cards.title: A day with western lowland gorillas
cards.summary: Western lowland gorillas live in forests in central Africa. They walk on the ground a great deal, often resting their weight on their knuckles.

cards.title: A ferret that depends on prairie dogs
cards.summary: A black-footed ferret may spend much of the day underground in tunnels dug by prairie dogs. It also hunts prairie dogs for food, following them through narrow passages where larger animals could not fit.

cards.title: A giant lizard from Indonesian islands
cards.summary: The Komodo dragon is a real animal found on a few islands in Indonesia. It is the largest kind of lizard alive today.

cards.title: A light-year measures distance
cards.summary: Light travels so quickly that in one second it can cover about 300,000 kilometers in empty space. But stars are so far apart that even light takes years to move between them.

cards.title: A red panda’s life in the trees
cards.summary: Look carefully at a branch in an Asian mountain forest and a red panda might be resting around it. This small mammal has reddish fur and a ringed tail.

cards.title: Algeria
cards.summary: Algeria is the largest country in Africa by land area. Algiers, the capital, lies on its Mediterranean coast in the far north.

cards.title: Altitude
cards.summary: Altitude describes how high something is compared with a chosen level. Maps often measure land height from sea level.

cards.title: Amazon River
cards.summary: The Amazon begins with streams in the Andes and grows as more rivers join it on the way east. Rain falling across a wide part of South America feeds its huge river system.

cards.title: Andes Mountains
cards.summary: The Andes run like a high spine along the western side of South America. Far below the coast, a large piece of the ocean floor slides beneath the edge of the continent.

cards.title: Antarctic Ice Sheet
cards.summary: Most of Antarctica is covered by a layer of ice thick enough to hide mountains and valleys beneath it. It formed as falling snow piled up over a very long time, squashing the air out of older layers and turning them into ice.

cards.title: Apollo 11, the first Moon landing
cards.summary: In July 1969, three people traveled to the Moon on Apollo 11. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin rode a small lander called Eagle down to the surface.

cards.title: Are orcas a kind of dolphin?
cards.summary: An orca, also called a killer whale, is the biggest member of the dolphin family. It has teeth, and what it catches depends on the group it lives with.

cards.title: Are your bones alive?
cards.summary: A dried bone in a museum can make it seem as if bones are just hard sticks. Inside you, each bone contains living cells.

cards.title: Argentina
cards.summary: Argentina runs down the eastern side of the Andes for much of southern South America. Near Buenos Aires, the capital, the land opens into grassy plains called the Pampas.

cards.title: Asteroids, the rocks between planets
cards.summary: An asteroid is a rocky or metal-rich object that moves around the Sun. Many asteroids are found between Mars and Jupiter, in a wide area called the asteroid belt.

cards.title: Atoms, the tiny pieces of matter
cards.summary: Air, water, rocks, and your own body are made of pieces called atoms. They are far too small to see with your eyes.

cards.title: Australia
cards.summary: Australia is a country in the Southern Hemisphere. Much of the middle is dry.

cards.title: Austria
cards.summary: If you cross Austria from west to east, the tall ridges of the Alps give way to lower land around Vienna, the capital. The Danube flows through Vienna and continues toward the Black Sea, passing through or beside several countries.

cards.title: Bangladesh
cards.summary: Much of Bangladesh sits on the low land where several large Asian rivers meet and flow into the Bay of Bengal. Water and silt from far away in the Himalayas can reach the fields and channels of this delta.

cards.title: Bats and how they find their way
cards.summary: Bats are mammals and can fly by flapping their wings. Their wings are made of thin skin stretched over long fingers.

cards.title: Belgium
cards.summary: Belgium sits between France, the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and the North Sea. Flat land near the coast gives way to higher, wooded country in the southeast.

cards.title: Belize
cards.summary: Belize faces the Caribbean Sea on the eastern side of Central America. A long coral reef lies offshore, with small islands, shallow water, and much deeper sea not far apart.

cards.title: Bhutan
cards.summary: Bhutan lies in the eastern Himalayas between India and China. Along the south, lower hills rise above the plains of India.

cards.title: Bolivia
cards.summary: Bolivia’s landscapes include high mountains, a wide plateau called the Altiplano, and low land toward the Amazon basin. In the west, the country shares Lake Titicaca with Peru.

cards.title: Botswana
cards.summary: Botswana is a mostly flat country in southern Africa with no sea coast. The Kalahari drylands cover much of it, but the northwest holds the Okavango Delta, where a river spreads across low ground instead of flowing into an ocean.

cards.title: Brazil
cards.summary: Brazil is the largest country in South America by area. Its eastern edge is along the Atlantic Ocean.

cards.title: Brunei
cards.summary: Brunei is a small country on the north coast of the island of Borneo. Its capital, Bandar Seri Begawan, stands beside the Brunei River near the coast.

cards.title: Bulgaria
cards.summary: Bulgaria lies in southeastern Europe, with the Black Sea on the east side and part of the Danube along the north. The Balkan Mountains cross the middle of the country from west to east.

cards.title: Callisto’s crater-covered surface
cards.summary: Pictures of Jupiter’s moon Callisto show round marks almost everywhere. Rocks and pieces of ice struck the surface long ago, leaving wide bowls called craters.

cards.title: Cambodia
cards.summary: Cambodia includes a broad low plain linked to the Mekong River. Its capital, Phnom Penh, grew near rivers that meet close together.

cards.title: Can a poem have no rhyme scheme?
cards.summary: A free verse poem does not have to follow a fixed rhyme pattern or a set number of beats per line. The writer can still plan where each line ends, how sounds repeat, and which words call for a pause.

cards.title: Can a porcupine throw its quills?
cards.summary: A North American porcupine does not toss its quills across the air. The quills are stiff hairs that come loose if an animal bumps into them.

cards.title: Can something in a free game cost real money?
cards.summary: You can start some games without paying, but they may offer extra colors, characters, or game coins for sale. Some coins are earned by playing.

cards.title: Canada
cards.summary: Canada covers a large part of North America, from the Atlantic Ocean in the east to the Pacific Ocean in the west and the Arctic Ocean to the north. A trip across it can take you through rocky mountains, broad plains, forests, and lakes.

cards.title: Caribbean Sea
cards.summary: The Caribbean Sea is a warm part of the Atlantic between Central America, northern South America, and a chain of islands. Cuba, Jamaica, and Hispaniola sit near its northern side.

cards.title: Ceres, a dwarf planet in the asteroid belt
cards.summary: Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt. Among all its rocky bodies is Ceres, a round world much larger than its neighbors.

cards.title: Chile
cards.summary: Chile is a remarkably long and narrow country between the Andes and the Pacific Ocean. Its northern Atacama Desert is so dry that some places rarely see rain.

cards.title: China
cards.summary: China covers a large part of eastern Asia. Its land generally steps down from high plateaus and mountains in the west to broad lowlands and a long coast in the east.

cards.title: Colombia
cards.summary: Colombia is in the northwest corner of South America. It is the continent’s only country with coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea.

cards.title: Costa Rica
cards.summary: Costa Rica runs between the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea in Central America. Mountains and volcanoes rise through the middle, and San José, the capital, is in the central part of the country.

cards.title: Croatia
cards.summary: Croatia curves around part of the Adriatic Sea. On the coast, many islands lie just offshore and some long ones run roughly the same direction as the shore.

cards.title: Cuba
cards.summary: Cuba is an island country at the northern edge of the Caribbean. The largest island stretches far from west to east, and many smaller islands and reefs lie nearby.

cards.title: Czechia
cards.summary: Czechia, also called the Czech Republic, sits in central Europe and has no coast. It contains the historic regions of Bohemia and Moravia and part of Silesia.

cards.title: Denmark
cards.summary: Denmark connects with mainland Europe through the Jutland Peninsula, which borders Germany. Much of the rest of the country is on islands.

cards.title: Density and why some things float
cards.summary: If you have two blocks the same size, one may feel much heavier. More matter is packed into that block’s space, so it is denser.

cards.title: Do genes decide exactly how tall you will be?
cards.summary: One gene cannot tell you exactly how tall you will become. Lots of small differences in inherited information can influence how a person grows.

cards.title: Do sunflowers turn to follow the Sun?
cards.summary: A young sunflower may face east in the morning and turn westward by late afternoon. One side of its stem grows faster than the other at different times, bending the plant as it grows.

cards.title: Do you need to add numbers to solve Sudoku?
cards.summary: A common Sudoku puzzle has nine rows, nine columns, and nine little squares containing nine spaces each. Put the digits one through nine into the empty spaces so each digit appears once in every row, column, and little square.

cards.title: Do your cells have DNA outside the nucleus?
cards.summary: Most of the DNA in a body cell stays in the nucleus. There is also a small amount in some little cell parts called mitochondria.

cards.title: Dominican Republic
cards.summary: The Dominican Republic covers the eastern part of Hispaniola, sharing that island with Haiti. Its capital, Santo Domingo, is on the Caribbean coast, on the south side of the island.

cards.title: Earth, our home planet
cards.summary: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only place where we know life exists. Most of its surface is covered by water.

cards.title: Earth’s moving plates
cards.summary: Earth’s stiff outer shell is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates. They fit together a little like puzzle pieces, but they move very slowly.

cards.title: Ecuador
cards.summary: Ecuador takes its name from the equator, the imaginary line that crosses the country. Quito, the capital, sits high in the Andes, where the elevation keeps conditions cooler than people might expect near that line.

cards.title: Egypt
cards.summary: Egypt is a country mostly in northeastern Africa. Much of its land is desert, while fields and cities lie along the Nile River.

cards.title: El Salvador
cards.summary: El Salvador lies on the Pacific side of Central America. Unlike many of its neighbors, it has no Caribbean coast.

cards.title: Enceladus, the moon that sprays ice
cards.summary: Ice covers the small moon Enceladus, but a salty ocean lies deep beneath it. Near the south pole, cracks release jets of water vapor and ice grains.

cards.title: Energy from heat inside Earth
cards.summary: Earth stays warm inside, and in some places there is hot water or steam deep underground. Wells can bring that heat to the surface.

cards.title: Estonia
cards.summary: Estonia is the northernmost of the three countries often grouped as the Baltic states. Tallinn, the capital, stands on the Gulf of Finland.

cards.title: Ethiopia
cards.summary: Ethiopia is a landlocked country in eastern Africa. Much of its central and northern land forms a broad highland split by deep valleys.

cards.title: Europa’s hidden ocean
cards.summary: Europa looks like an ice-covered ball scratched with long lines. Scientists think much of the ice sits above a global ocean of salty water.

cards.title: Exoplanets, worlds around other stars
cards.summary: A planet beyond our solar system is called an exoplanet. Many circle stars much like our planets circle the Sun.

cards.title: Fiji
cards.summary: Fiji is a group of islands in the South Pacific. The two largest, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, have hills and valleys, while many smaller islands sit close to coral reefs.

cards.title: Finland
cards.summary: Finland has thousands of lakes, many among forests in the southern and central parts of the country. In the last ice age, moving ice scoured the ground.

cards.title: France
cards.summary: Most of France’s land is in western Europe. Paris, its capital, grew along the Seine River.

cards.title: Galápagos Islands
cards.summary: The Galápagos Islands lie far west of Ecuador’s mainland in the Pacific. Eruptions built the islands from the seafloor, so they were separated from the continent from the start.

cards.title: Galaxies and the Milky Way
cards.summary: A galaxy is an enormous group of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity. Some galaxies have swirling arms, others look like smooth blobs, and some have no neat shape.

cards.title: Ganymede, the largest moon
cards.summary: Ganymede goes around Jupiter and is the largest moon in our solar system. It is wider than the planet Mercury, although it has much less mass.

cards.title: Germany
cards.summary: Germany stretches from low country on the North Sea and Baltic Sea to mountains near the Alps. Its capital, Berlin, is in the northeast.

cards.title: Ghana
cards.summary: Ghana faces the Gulf of Guinea in western Africa. Accra, the capital, lies beside the sea, and the land stretches inland to drier plains in the north.

cards.title: Grand Canyon
cards.summary: The Grand Canyon is a huge cut through rock in northern Arizona. Far below its rim, the Colorado River has been lifting and carrying away pieces of rock for millions of years.

cards.title: Gravity, the pull between objects
cards.summary: Gravity is a pull between objects that have mass. A ball falls to the floor because Earth pulls it down.

cards.title: Great Barrier Reef
cards.summary: The Great Barrier Reef lies off Australia’s northeastern coast. It is made of thousands of separate reefs rather than one long unbroken wall.

cards.title: Greece
cards.summary: Greece lies at the southern end of the Balkan Peninsula, and its land reaches far into the sea through islands and smaller peninsulas. Athens, the capital, is on the mainland near the coast.

cards.title: Guatemala
cards.summary: Guatemala reaches south from Mexico into Central America. It has low forested country in the north and a chain of mountains and volcanoes closer to the Pacific.

cards.title: Guyana
cards.summary: Guyana lies on the Atlantic side of northern South America, east of Venezuela and west of Suriname. Much of its population lives on the narrow coastal plain, where Georgetown, the capital, stands near the mouth of the Demerara River.

cards.title: Haiti
cards.summary: Haiti covers the western part of Hispaniola, an island it shares with the Dominican Republic. Its capital, Port-au-Prince, sits beside a sheltered bay on the western side.

cards.title: Himalayas
cards.summary: The Himalayas stretch across southern Asia and contain many of Earth’s highest mountains. They started growing when the land carrying India pushed into the land to the north.

cards.title: Honduras
cards.summary: Honduras has a long coast on the Caribbean Sea and a much shorter coast beside the Gulf of Fonseca, which opens to the Pacific. Mountains take up much of the land between the two sides.

cards.title: How a beaver makes a pond
cards.summary: A beaver can turn a shallow stream into a pond by piling branches and mud across it. Water slows down behind the dam and spreads into a wider area.

cards.title: How a capacitor holds a burst of energy
cards.summary: A capacitor can hold energy by keeping opposite charges apart. Many capacitors have two pieces of metal separated by a very thin layer that does not let charge pass easily.

cards.title: How a door knows someone is coming
cards.summary: An automatic door often uses a sensor to look for movement near the entrance. Some sensors send out radio waves and notice a change when those waves bounce off a moving person.

cards.title: How a generator makes electric current
cards.summary: In many generators, a magnet moves past loops of wire, or the wire moves inside a magnetic field. The changing field can cause electric charges to move through the wire.

cards.title: How a heat pump moves warmth
cards.summary: A heat pump moves heat using a liquid that easily changes into a gas. The fluid absorbs heat as it becomes gas in one part of the machine.

cards.title: How a jet engine pushes a plane forward
cards.summary: One kind of jet engine pulls air in and squeezes it through a row of spinning blades. Fuel burns in the crowded air and heats it.

cards.title: How a machine digs a tunnel
cards.summary: One way to dig a tunnel is with a round machine that cuts through earth or rock as it advances. Its head breaks the material into small pieces.

cards.title: How a magnetic compass points a direction
cards.summary: A compass has a magnetic needle that can turn with little friction. Earth has a magnetic field that gives the needle a direction.

cards.title: How a phone can find its position using satellites
cards.summary: Navigation satellites broadcast radio signals that say where the satellites are and when the signals left. A receiver compares the signal times.

cards.title: How a ratchet clicks in one direction
cards.summary: A ratchet has a row of teeth and a piece that catches against them. On each tooth, one face is sloped.

cards.title: How a solar eclipse works
cards.summary: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon crosses in front of the Sun as seen from part of Earth. The Moon’s shadow falls on a patch of Earth.

cards.title: How a spacecraft brought asteroid rocks to Earth
cards.summary: The OSIRIS-REx mission sent a spacecraft to the asteroid Bennu. It studied the surface from nearby before choosing a sampling spot.

cards.title: How a spacesuit keeps an astronaut alive
cards.summary: Outside a spacecraft there is almost no air. A spacesuit for spacewalks is like a tiny spacecraft that moves with a person.

cards.title: How a star grows into a red giant
cards.summary: A star like the Sun spends much of its life joining hydrogen in its center to make helium and give off energy. Eventually its center runs low on hydrogen.

cards.title: How a stovetop can heat the pan directly
cards.summary: Under the surface of an induction cooktop is a coil of wire. A changing current in the coil makes a changing magnetic field.

cards.title: How a subway carries people across a city
cards.summary: A subway runs trains frequently between stations where many people want to travel. Tunnels let the railway go below busy streets, but some sections may run outside or on bridges.

cards.title: How a suspension bridge hangs from cables
cards.summary: On a suspension bridge, smaller vertical lines hang the roadway from large curved cables. Towers support the high points of those cables.

cards.title: How a telescope can listen for radio waves
cards.summary: A radio telescope gathers radio waves from space. Many use a large curved metal dish that sends incoming waves toward a receiver, the way a mirror can bring visible light to a focus.

cards.title: How a tiny LED makes light
cards.summary: An LED is a small electronic part made from special solid materials. When electric current goes through it in the intended direction, charges inside can give some of their energy away as light.

cards.title: How a tower crane lifts a heavy load
cards.summary: A tower crane lifts a load by winding a cable onto a drum. Near the hook, several lengths of cable may share the weight with a group of pulleys.

cards.title: How a traffic light can detect a waiting car
cards.summary: Some traffic lights follow a schedule, while others can change when a vehicle is waiting. One kind of detector uses wire arranged in a loop under the road.

cards.title: How a train can float over its guideway
cards.summary: A maglev train uses magnets to lift and guide it instead of ordinary wheels doing all the work. Some designs carry magnets on the train that interact with electric coils along the track.

cards.title: How a wedge pushes things apart
cards.summary: A wedge is thick at one end and tapers toward the other. As its narrow end moves into a gap, its sloping sides force the two surfaces apart.

cards.title: How a wheel and axle work together
cards.summary: A wheel and axle can turn as one piece even though the wheel is wider than the axle. A door knob is a good example.

cards.title: How a whole star can leave a city-sized object
cards.summary: When some massive stars run out of fuel, their centers squeeze down and the outer material blows away. If the collapsed center survives without becoming a black hole, it may become a neutron star.

cards.title: How an alligator lives on land and in water
cards.summary: An American alligator can float with much of its body hidden below the surface. Its eyes and nostrils sit high enough to stay above the water while it waits.

cards.title: How an arch bridge carries weight
cards.summary: An arch bridge uses a curved shape to carry loads toward the ground at each end. The stones in a traditional arch lean on one another, so the weight mainly squeezes them together.

cards.title: How an electric car moves and recharges
cards.summary: An electric car stores energy in a large battery. An electric motor turns the wheels to make the car move.

cards.title: How an electric circuit makes a light work
cards.summary: An electric circuit gives electric charges a path to move along. In a simple flashlight, the battery, bulb, and wires can make a loop.

cards.title: How an electromagnet turns magnetism on and off
cards.summary: When current runs through a wire, it makes a magnetic field around it. Winding the wire into a coil lets the fields of many loops work together.

cards.title: How an elevator goes up and down
cards.summary: Many elevators hang the car from strong ropes or belts over a powered wheel. A counterweight hangs on the opposite side and helps balance the car’s weight.

cards.title: How are triangles different from one another?
cards.summary: Every triangle has three straight sides and three corners. Some triangles have three equal sides.

cards.title: How atoms join to make molecules
cards.summary: A molecule is a group of atoms joined together. One water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

cards.title: How big can a giant sequoia get?
cards.summary: A giant sequoia builds a trunk wide enough to make people standing beside it look tiny. It is famous for the amount of wood in that trunk.

cards.title: How can 1/2 and 2/4 be equal?
cards.summary: Draw two strips of the same length. Divide one into two equal parts and shade one part.

cards.title: How can a banana grow without big seeds?
cards.summary: A wild banana can have hard, noticeable seeds, but the Cavendish bananas sold in many stores usually have no mature seeds. The fruit can grow without the usual process of making seeds.

cards.title: How can a bean be a pod or a seed on your plate?
cards.summary: A bean plant grows long pods around its seeds. In green beans, people often eat the soft pods along with young seeds.

cards.title: How can a big drum be tuned to a note?
cards.summary: Timpani are bowl-shaped drums with skins or plastic heads stretched across their tops. Strike the drum with a soft-headed stick, and its stretched surface makes a clear note.

cards.title: How can a cocoon become a silk thread?
cards.summary: A silkworm spins a long strand around itself before it changes into a moth. Layers of that strand form the cocoon.

cards.title: How can a color show whether something is acidic?
cards.summary: Some coloring substances take on different colors in acidic and basic liquids. We call a substance used this way an indicator.

cards.title: How can a computer notice what is happening around it?
cards.summary: A sensor is a part that notices or measures something. On a robot it could measure how much light is coming from a direction, or notice when a wheel has turned.

cards.title: How can a computer read a screen aloud?
cards.summary: A screen reader is software that tells a person about what is on a screen. It can speak the words in a menu or say the name of the button a person might press next.

cards.title: How can a computer store a sound?
cards.summary: Sound can make a microphone create a changing electrical signal. To hold a recording, a device can measure that signal again and again at very short steps in time.

cards.title: How can a fire change which plants grow in a forest?
cards.summary: Fire may harm trees and animals, but some ecosystems developed with fires from time to time. In some forests, fires remove low plants that compete for sunlight.

cards.title: How can a fungus help a plant root?
cards.summary: Some fungi grow right against plant roots or inside parts of the roots. Their thin threads can reach more ground than the root could cover by itself.

cards.title: How can a greenhouse grow plants when it is cold outside?
cards.summary: Clear parts of a greenhouse let sunlight reach the plants and surfaces inside. The light can warm those surfaces.

cards.title: How can a hill decide which river gets the rain?
cards.summary: A watershed is an area where water drains toward the same river, lake, or other low place. Rain falling on opposite sides of a ridge may reach different streams.

cards.title: How can a lake make extra snow?
cards.summary: Cold air blowing over a stretch of unfrozen lake picks up heat and water vapor from the water. The warmed, moister air rises and cools.

cards.title: How can a password manager help a family?
cards.summary: It can be hard to remember a different long password for every account. A password manager can keep a protected list.

cards.title: How can a pile of oysters become a reef again?
cards.summary: An oyster can attach to a hard object. If many oysters grow next to and on top of one another, their shells form a rough structure with cracks and ledges.

cards.title: How can a prefix or suffix change a word?
cards.summary: Some words have parts that help you guess the meaning. The beginning part in “rewrite” is re-, which often means again.

cards.title: How can a printer build an object you can pick up?
cards.summary: A 3D printer can turn a computer model into a solid object. Its program pictures the model as many very thin horizontal layers.

cards.title: How can a printer use the same letters in different books?
cards.summary: Movable type uses small pieces with letters or other signs on their faces. A printer sets the pieces in a frame to make lines of writing, puts ink on them, and presses them against paper.

cards.title: How can a program find something in a sorted list?
cards.summary: Think of looking for the number 82 in a long row of cards already in order. You can look at the card in the middle.

cards.title: How can a program make a choice?
cards.summary: A program can follow different instructions depending on what has happened. A game can ask whether the player has reached the end of a path.

cards.title: How can a program put a list in order?
cards.summary: To order a pile of numbered cards, you could make a short row and slide each new card into its place. If the row says 2, 4, and 8, a new card with 5 goes after 4.

cards.title: How can a quilt tell a story?
cards.summary: Artist Faith Ringgold made artworks that brought pictures, words, and fabric together. A story quilt can have a picture in the middle and written pieces around it, with patterned cloth framing what you read and see.

cards.title: How can a river carve a deep canyon?
cards.summary: Water carrying sand and stones can wear away the bottom of a riverbed. Over a very long time a river may cut much deeper into the land.

cards.title: How can a rock float?
cards.summary: Pumice forms when particular kinds of melted rock have gas bubbles in them as they cool. After the rock hardens, it is full of holes where bubbles used to be.

cards.title: How can a snowflake turn into an ice pellet?
cards.summary: Snow may start falling through air cold enough to keep it frozen. Sometimes a layer of warmer air farther down partly melts the flakes.

cards.title: How can a solid rock change without melting?
cards.summary: A rock buried deep underground can warm up and be squeezed hard. Minerals may change shape or grow again, and new minerals may appear.

cards.title: How can a whole river of ice move?
cards.summary: When more snow falls each year than melts, layers can build up. The weight presses the snow below into dense ice.

cards.title: How can an animal leave a fossil without leaving a bone?
cards.summary: A track in soft mud can fill in with sand. Later, the mud and sand can harden into rock.

cards.title: How can an animal make its own light?
cards.summary: Some living things can give off light by mixing chemicals inside their bodies. That light is called bioluminescence.

cards.title: How can an animal return to a place where it disappeared?
cards.summary: A species may disappear from one place while still living somewhere else. Reintroduction means bringing some back to a suitable place in its former range.

cards.title: How can an idea become a federal law?
cards.summary: A member of Congress can put an idea into a written proposal called a bill. A small group in the House or Senate can study it, hear from people, and suggest changes.

cards.title: How can cabbage and cauliflower be close relatives?
cards.summary: Cabbage and cauliflower look different because growers choose plants for different parts. Many cabbages make a ball of closely packed leaves.

cards.title: How can cream turn into butter?
cards.summary: Cream contains many small drops of milk fat in a watery liquid. Churning moves the cream around until more of the drops bump together and stick.

cards.title: How can deep-sea life make food without sunlight?
cards.summary: At some deep-sea vents, tiny living things can use energy from chemicals in the water to make food. They do not have to catch light from the Sun.

cards.title: How can dry earth become a wall?
cards.summary: Builders can mix earth with water and shape it into adobe bricks. The bricks dry in the air and sun before people place them in a wall.

cards.title: How can egg white turn into a fluffy foam?
cards.summary: Whipping egg white draws air into the liquid and breaks it into many small bubbles. Some of the proteins in the egg white unfold and collect near the bubbles, helping build a thin film that keeps them from popping so fast.

cards.title: How can graphite and diamond both be carbon?
cards.summary: A piece of graphite and a diamond can both be made of carbon atoms. In graphite, carbon atoms connect in layers.

cards.title: How can hungry sea otters help a kelp forest?
cards.summary: Sea otters float on their backs and can hold food above the water as they eat. Some use a stone to open a hard shell.

cards.title: How can invisible air press on things?
cards.summary: Air is made of moving molecules that bump into your skin and other surfaces all the time. Those tiny pushes add up to air pressure.

cards.title: How can moss grow without true roots?
cards.summary: Mosses are small plants that often make soft green mats. Instead of true roots, many have tiny threads that hold the plant in place.

cards.title: How can mud, sand, or shells become rock?
cards.summary: Sand, mud, and pieces of shells can settle when moving water or air slows down. A new layer may cover an older one.

cards.title: How can people have different versions of a gene?
cards.summary: Imagine looking up the same short passage in two copies of a book and finding a letter that is different. A related thing can happen in DNA.

cards.title: How can plants grow without soil?
cards.summary: A plant needs water, minerals, light and suitable air, but it may not have to get those supplies from soil. In hydroponics, a grower can send water with dissolved nutrients to the roots.

cards.title: How can sand become glass?
cards.summary: A lot of familiar glass starts with sand rich in a material called silica. Glassmakers add other ingredients and heat the mix until it can flow.

cards.title: How can seaweed make an underwater forest?
cards.summary: Giant kelp grows upward from rocks on the sea bottom. It is a kind of large brown algae.

cards.title: How can shading make a picture look solid?
cards.summary: A ball under a lamp has a bright part facing the lamp and a darker part turned away from it. An artist can draw those changes in lightness inside a flat circle so it looks like a ball.

cards.title: How can small pieces make a big picture?
cards.summary: Mosaics use small pieces of glass, stone, or another material arranged into a picture or pattern. Each piece can cover just a little bit of the final surface.

cards.title: How can stacks of dots show measurements?
cards.summary: A dot plot can show measurements along a marked number line. Place one dot above the right number for each measurement.

cards.title: How can there be water beneath the ground?
cards.summary: Some rain soaks through soil into openings between grains or into cracks in rock. If enough of those openings connect, water can move through them.

cards.title: How can things that lived in the sea become limestone?
cards.summary: Some limestone begins with bits of shells and other hard parts from life in water. The bits settle to the bottom and build layers.

cards.title: How can two different languages be related?
cards.summary: Languages can change a little as people pass them on. Groups sometimes move apart and use language in different ways, generation after generation.

cards.title: How can two lights work separately on one battery?
cards.summary: Imagine two lamps connected so each has its own path between the battery’s ends. Electricity can travel in both branches of this parallel circuit.

cards.title: How can you build a garden in shallow water?
cards.summary: In the lakes near the old Aztec capital, farmers made raised beds called chinampas. Mud and plant material helped build up long plots with canals between them.

cards.title: How can you count syllables in a word?
cards.summary: A syllable is one sound part of a spoken word. Say rainbow slowly and listen for two parts, rain and bow.

cards.title: How can you estimate an answer?
cards.summary: An estimate is a sensible guess based on what you know. Suppose you are adding 29 stickers, 42 stickers, and 38 stickers.

cards.title: How can you predict the next part of a pattern?
cards.summary: Read these colors aloud: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue. The smallest block that keeps repeating is red, blue, blue.

cards.title: How can you spot an advertisement in a game or video?
cards.summary: An ad tries to make people interested in a product, game, or service. It can look like a separate sign.

cards.title: How can you tell a chemical reaction happened?
cards.summary: A chemical reaction happens when starting substances change into different substances. Their atoms are arranged in new ways.

cards.title: How can you tell a harbor seal from a sea lion?
cards.summary: A harbor seal has small ear openings behind its eyes, but lacks the outer ear flaps you can see on a sea lion. Its short front flippers and its rear flippers help it steer and swim.

cards.title: How can you tell how much time has passed?
cards.summary: Elapsed time is how long something lasts from start to finish. Suppose you begin reading at 2:45 and stop at 3:20.

cards.title: How can you tell which things are farther away?
cards.summary: Hold two fingers up with one a little in front of the other. Look with one eye and then with the other.

cards.title: How can your eyes tell colors apart?
cards.summary: Many people have three kinds of cone cell near the back of each eye. Each kind reacts most strongly to a different range of light.

cards.title: How canal locks raise and lower boats
cards.summary: A lock is a short section of water with gates at both ends. A boat enters while the lock’s water matches the level outside the open gate.

cards.title: How clouds form
cards.summary: A cloud is a group of very small water drops, ice crystals, or both. Air can carry water as an invisible gas called water vapor.

cards.title: How could Gothic builders make room for tall windows?
cards.summary: Medieval Gothic builders used pointed arches, ribs along ceilings, and strong supports outside some high walls. Together, these features helped carry the weight of the stone and reduce some of the pressure on parts of the wall.

cards.title: How could knots record numbers?
cards.summary: People in the Andes kept records using sets of cords called quipus. A main cord might hold many hanging cords.

cards.title: How could people travel the Inca road without modern machines?
cards.summary: The Inca connected many existing routes and built new roads through western South America. Builders used stone steps or walls where a path climbed a slope.

cards.title: How could Viking longships travel by sail or by oar?
cards.summary: Some Viking Age sailors used long, narrow boats moved by a sail or by oars. A crew could row if the wind did not help, and it could use the sail for longer trips in a favorable wind.

cards.title: How curved lenses bend light
cards.summary: A straw looks bent in water because light from it changes direction when it crosses from water into air at an angle. This is called refraction.

cards.title: How dams hold and release water
cards.summary: A dam is a barrier built across a valley or a river. Water gathers behind it in a reservoir.

cards.title: How did a city grow on a lake?
cards.summary: Tenochtitlan was the Aztec capital. It grew on islands and shallow land in a lake where Mexico City stands today.

cards.title: How did a map help start Treasure Island?
cards.summary: Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson made a drawing of an island and used it to imagine a story. In Treasure Island, the map gives characters a reason to travel and a place to search.

cards.title: How did Aksum become a powerful trading kingdom?
cards.summary: Aksum was a center of an ancient kingdom in what is now northern Ethiopia. Its routes linked highland towns with ports and the wider trade of the Red Sea.

cards.title: How did Allosaurus bite its food?
cards.summary: Allosaurus was a big predator during the Jurassic Period. Its teeth curved backward and had tiny notches along the edges.

cards.title: How did Alma Thomas make pictures out of patches of color?
cards.summary: Alma Thomas painted groups of bright marks that can look as if they are moving in rows, rings, or streams. Small spaces between the marks let quieter colors show.

cards.title: How did Babylon become a great ancient city?
cards.summary: Babylon stood on the Euphrates River in what is now Iraq. It was a center of power more than once.

cards.title: How did basketball begin?
cards.summary: James Naismith invented basketball in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1891. He was looking for a game people could play indoors in winter.

cards.title: How did Beatrix Potter put real animals into stories?
cards.summary: Beatrix Potter watched real animals closely before drawing animals who wore clothes and had adventures in her stories. She kept rabbits and other small animals when she was young.

cards.title: How did Benjamin Franklin help people share books and ideas?
cards.summary: Benjamin Franklin worked as a printer in Philadelphia before he became a famous public figure. Printing helped him share news and ideas with readers.

cards.title: How did Brachiosaurus reach high leaves?
cards.summary: Brachiosaurus had long front legs that lifted its shoulders higher than its hips. From that sloping body, a long neck reached upward, so the animal could have gathered leaves well above the height most dinosaurs could reach.

cards.title: How did builders fit a huge crowd into the Colosseum?
cards.summary: Rome’s Colosseum was an oval arena with rows of seats rising around the central floor. Visitors entered through many ground-level openings.

cards.title: How did Carthage become a sea power?
cards.summary: Carthage began as a settlement founded by Phoenician seafarers on the North African shore, near modern Tunis. A harbor close to routes across the Mediterranean made it a useful place to trade.

cards.title: How did cities change in Song China?
cards.summary: During the Song dynasty, people in Chinese cities bought goods from shops and markets and read books printed in growing numbers. Printing with carved blocks let a maker produce many pages from the same design.

cards.title: How did Duke Ellington write for his band?
cards.summary: Duke Ellington led a jazz orchestra and wrote music it could play. He knew the different voices of the people in his band, so a part for one player could sound different from a part for another on the same kind of instrument.

cards.title: How did E. B. White make a farm story feel real?
cards.summary: E. B.

cards.title: How did Ella Fitzgerald use her voice like an instrument?
cards.summary: Ella Fitzgerald was a jazz singer known for the care she took with pitch and rhythm. At times she sang syllables without ordinary words, choosing sounds such as short pulses or long notes.

cards.title: How did Frederick Douglass use speeches and writing to change minds?
cards.summary: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery and became a writer and public speaker. He described his own experiences so readers could understand how slavery harmed people and took away their choices.

cards.title: How did Georgia O’Keeffe make small things feel huge?
cards.summary: Georgia O’Keeffe painted flowers, hills, bones, buildings, and other things she looked at closely. In some flower paintings, a small petal fills a large part of the picture.

cards.title: How did Haiti become an independent country?
cards.summary: France once ruled a colony in the western part of the island of Hispaniola, where many people were enslaved on plantations. In 1791, enslaved people began a large uprising.

cards.title: How did Harriet Tubman help people reach freedom?
cards.summary: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery in Maryland. She then returned many times to help family members and other people escape, using connections along the Underground Railroad.

cards.title: How did Ida B. Wells use facts to fight injustice?
cards.summary: Ida B. Wells was a teacher and journalist.

cards.title: How did Inca builders use a steep mountain ridge?
cards.summary: Machu Picchu is an Inca site high in the Andes of present-day Peru. Its builders made terraces to create level strips of land on steep slopes.

cards.title: How did Langston Hughes bring music into poetry?
cards.summary: Langston Hughes wrote poetry, plays, and stories about Black life in the United States. He listened to the sounds of blues and jazz and used some of their rhythms and patterns in poems.

cards.title: How did M. C. Escher make shapes fit together?
cards.summary: M. C.

cards.title: How did Maya writers put sounds and words into pictures?
cards.summary: Ancient Maya writing used signs called glyphs. A glyph might stand for a whole word, or it might stand for a sound like the beginning of a word.

cards.title: How did Nelson Mandela help change South Africa?
cards.summary: Nelson Mandela helped organize against apartheid, the system that denied many people equal rights in South Africa. He spent many years in prison.

cards.title: How did older cities start to build skyscrapers?
cards.summary: In a building with heavy stone walls, the walls near the ground can become very thick as more floors are added. Builders in the late 1800s began giving tall buildings strong frames made of metal.

cards.title: How did people build homes inside cliffs at Mesa Verde?
cards.summary: Ancestral Pueblo people farmed and lived in the Mesa Verde region of what is now Colorado. Some later homes were tucked under wide shelves in sandstone cliffs.

cards.title: How did people build the city of Mohenjo-daro?
cards.summary: Mohenjo-daro was an ancient city in the Indus region of what is now Pakistan. Builders arranged many houses along streets and lanes.

cards.title: How did people keep a bus boycott going for more than a year?
cards.summary: Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, organized a boycott of the city buses in 1955 after Rosa Parks’s arrest. Many people walked, shared rides, or used carpools to keep going to work and school.

cards.title: How did people live in ancient Egypt?
cards.summary: In ancient Egypt, much of daily life followed the Nile River. Flooding once left rich mud across nearby fields.

cards.title: How did people turn plant material into paper?
cards.summary: To make many kinds of paper, people separate plant material into tiny strands, mix them with water, and lift a thin layer on a screen. As the water drains, the strands stay in a mat.

cards.title: How did Roman aqueducts carry water?
cards.summary: A Roman aqueduct carried water from a source, such as a spring, toward a place people needed it. Builders gave the water channel a gentle downhill slope so gravity kept the water moving.

cards.title: How did Rome govern itself before its emperors?
cards.summary: For several centuries Rome called itself a republic. Instead of having one king with the job for life, Rome used elected officials with shorter terms.

cards.title: How did Rome govern lands far beyond Italy?
cards.summary: Augustus gained control of Rome and its lands more than two thousand years ago. Rome’s empire stretched across large parts of Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa.

cards.title: How did Sacagawea help the Lewis and Clark expedition?
cards.summary: Sacagawea traveled with the group led by Lewis and Clark while carrying her young child. She could speak languages that helped the explorers communicate.

cards.title: How did Sequoyah make a way to write Cherokee?
cards.summary: Sequoyah developed signs to write the Cherokee language. Most of the signs let a reader recognize a spoken syllable at a time.

cards.title: How did the ancient Maya organize their cities?
cards.summary: Ancient Maya people built cities across parts of what are now Mexico and Central America. Each city and the lands around it could have its own ruler.

cards.title: How did the ancient Persian Empire govern faraway lands?
cards.summary: The Achaemenid kings ruled an empire that stretched from Egypt and western Asia toward the Indus region. A king could not visit every town to decide what should happen there.

cards.title: How did the Erie Canal move boats across New York?
cards.summary: Before railroads reached many places, the Erie Canal let boats carry goods between the Hudson River and Lake Erie. Crews dug long channels and built gates that could close off a section.

cards.title: How did the Inca rule across the Andes?
cards.summary: The Inca Empire stretched along the Andes of western South America before Spanish conquest. Its rulers governed from Cusco and linked many communities with roads.

cards.title: How did the modern Olympic Games begin?
cards.summary: The first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens, Greece, in 1896. Organizers drew inspiration from games held long before at Olympia.

cards.title: How did the Mongol Empire connect distant places?
cards.summary: Chinggis Khan united many groups on the grasslands of Inner Asia early in the thirteenth century. He and the rulers who followed him took control of lands far beyond those grasslands.

cards.title: How did the Nineteenth Amendment change voting?
cards.summary: The Nineteenth Amendment says that a U.S. citizen’s right to vote cannot be denied because of their sex.

cards.title: How did the Panama Canal change ocean travel?
cards.summary: Before the Panama Canal opened, ships traveling between the Atlantic and Pacific sides of the Americas often had to sail far around South America. Workers in Panama dug through hills, built dams, and made locks to raise ships to a lake and lower them again.

cards.title: How did the Qin form one Chinese empire?
cards.summary: Before the Qin empire, several powerful states competed for land in China. The Qin ruler defeated the others and called himself the First Emperor in 221 BCE.

cards.title: How did the Rosetta Stone help people read hieroglyphs?
cards.summary: The Rosetta Stone has the same announcement carved in three kinds of writing. One is in Greek, which scholars could already read.

cards.title: How did the Thirteenth Amendment change the Constitution?
cards.summary: The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery and forced labor across the United States, except as punishment after conviction for a crime. States approved it in 1865, when the Civil War was ending.

cards.title: How did thirteen colonies become a new country?
cards.summary: The thirteen British colonies on the Atlantic coast included people who disagreed about who should make laws and collect taxes. Protest turned into fighting in 1775.

cards.title: How did towns of the Swahili coast trade across the ocean?
cards.summary: For centuries, merchants from towns along the eastern coast of Africa traded across the Indian Ocean. Sailors learned when winds were likely to carry boats toward Africa or away from it.

cards.title: How did trade help the Mali Empire grow?
cards.summary: The Mali Empire grew in West Africa along routes that linked regions with very different useful goods. Gold came from parts of West Africa, and salt could be brought from mines in the Sahara.

cards.title: How did water shape the city of Angkor?
cards.summary: Angkor grew in a part of Southeast Asia where rain changes greatly between seasons. Khmer builders made channels and wide places that could hold water.

cards.title: How did workers connect rail lines across the United States?
cards.summary: In the 1860s, the Central Pacific built tracks east from California while the Union Pacific built west from the middle of the country. Workers cut paths, moved earth, laid rails, and carried heavy equipment across mountains and plains.

cards.title: How do a story’s events make a plot?
cards.summary: A plot is the set of events that make up a story and the ways they fit together. Imagine someone loses a lunchbox, checks the classroom, follows a clue, and finds it on the soccer field.

cards.title: How do airplane wings and tails steer?
cards.summary: An airplane can point its nose up or down, turn it left or right, or tip one wing lower than the other. Moving parts push on flowing air to help make these turns.

cards.title: How do Arabic letters change shape in a word?
cards.summary: Arabic writing usually runs from right to left. Many letters join their neighbors, so a letter may look somewhat different at the beginning, middle, or end of a word.

cards.title: How do bars show data?
cards.summary: A bar graph uses bars to show how much is in each group. Imagine surveying a class about favorite fruit.

cards.title: How do capillaries deliver oxygen to cells?
cards.summary: The larger blood vessels branch into tiny tubes called capillaries. Each tube has a very thin wall.

cards.title: How do chromosomes help pack DNA?
cards.summary: DNA is long and thin, and a cell is tiny. To pack DNA into that small space, the cell winds it around proteins and folds it further.

cards.title: How do comic panels tell a story?
cards.summary: A comic tells a story with pictures and sometimes words. Pictures can sit in separate boxes called panels.

cards.title: How do computers agree which letters to show?
cards.summary: A text program needs a shared way to know which letter or sign a stored number means. Unicode assigns a number to a letter, sign, or other text character.

cards.title: How do computers keep files without power?
cards.summary: A computer keeps some information in devices that are built to remember without power. They can hold drawings, recordings, and programs between uses.

cards.title: How do dominoes fit into a chain?
cards.summary: A domino is a tile marked into two halves. Each half can have dots or be blank.

cards.title: How do Egyptian hieroglyphs work?
cards.summary: Ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs are signs used to write the Egyptian language. Some are easy to recognize as pictures, such as an owl or an eye.

cards.title: How do evergreen trees stay green all year?
cards.summary: Evergreen plants keep some green leaves throughout the year. That does not mean that each leaf lasts forever.

cards.title: How do farmers water crops when it does not rain?
cards.summary: Irrigation means bringing water to a place where plants need it. A farm may get water from a river, a well, or a place where water has been stored.

cards.title: How do folders help you find files?
cards.summary: If all of your saved work were in one big pile, it could be hard to find a particular drawing. A folder lets you give a name to a group of files.

cards.title: How do fungi help a fallen log break down?
cards.summary: A fallen branch still has food materials locked inside its tough wood. Some fungi grow into the branch and release substances that break the wood down.

cards.title: How do groups of cells do bigger jobs?
cards.summary: A single cell can send a message, move, or carry a supply, but a large body needs many cells working in groups. A group of organized cells and the material around them forms a tissue.

cards.title: How do ice crystals grow on a window?
cards.summary: Frost can form when moist air touches a surface that is cold enough for water to turn directly from vapor into ice. The new ice can grow in delicate branches across a window or along a blade of grass.

cards.title: How do joints let your body move?
cards.summary: A joint is a place where bones meet. Many joints let one bone move against the other.

cards.title: How do leaves help a plant grow?
cards.summary: Leaves give many plants a wide surface to catch sunlight. A green leaf uses light, water and a gas from the air to make sugars.

cards.title: How do lungs get oxygen into your body?
cards.summary: When you breathe in, air travels down your windpipe and through branches that get smaller and smaller inside your lungs. At the ends of many branches are clusters of tiny air sacs.

cards.title: How do meters, centimeters, and kilometers fit together?
cards.summary: A meter is a unit of length. A centimeter is one hundredth of a meter, so a meter stick has a hundred centimeters along it.

cards.title: How do muscles move your bones?
cards.summary: When you bend your elbow, muscles near your upper arm put a pull on your bones. Strong strips called tendons attach many muscles to bones.

cards.title: How do musicians know how loudly to play?
cards.summary: Dynamics tell musicians how loud or soft their music should sound. A group may begin so softly that you can barely hear it, then grow louder until the whole room seems full.

cards.title: How do orchestra musicians play together?
cards.summary: An orchestra is a group of musicians who play different instruments together. A typical orchestra includes strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion.

cards.title: How do people read braille?
cards.summary: Braille uses patterns of raised dots. A reader feels them with their fingertips.

cards.title: How do programmers find and fix bugs?
cards.summary: A bug is a problem in a program. Imagine a score that goes up when the player should lose a point.

cards.title: How do red blood cells carry oxygen?
cards.summary: A red blood cell is a flexible, flat disc with thinner spots in its middle. It carries a substance called hemoglobin.

cards.title: How do researchers recognize a right whale?
cards.summary: A North Atlantic right whale has patches of rough skin on its head. Tiny animals live on those raised spots and can make them look white.

cards.title: How do rows help you multiply?
cards.summary: Imagine setting out three rows of four buttons. Each row has the same number, so you can count by fours or multiply three by four.

cards.title: How do scraps turn into compost?
cards.summary: A compost pile gives little animals and other living things a place to break down dead leaves, plant scraps and similar materials. They use some parts as food.

cards.title: How do screens mix red, green, and blue light?
cards.summary: Many screens create colors by mixing red, green, and blue light. A little spot on the screen can get a different amount of each color.

cards.title: How do seeds get far from the parent plant?
cards.summary: A seed often has a better chance to find space and light if it lands away from its parent. A dandelion makes tiny dry fruits that float in the breeze on little parachutes.

cards.title: How do stones surround space in Go?
cards.summary: Go is a board game in which two players take turns putting black and white stones where lines cross. Once a stone is placed, it stays there unless it is captured.

cards.title: How do taste buds tell flavors apart?
cards.summary: When you take a bite, tiny bits of dissolved food meet taste cells. Groups of such cells form taste buds.

cards.title: How do the faces of a box fit together?
cards.summary: A rectangular box has six flat faces. Each face meets its neighbor along an edge, and three edges come together at a corner.

cards.title: How do tiny fibers become a sheet of paper?
cards.summary: Many kinds of paper start with tiny wood fibers. A mill separates the fibers and mixes them with water, making a wet mass called pulp.

cards.title: How do watercolors make light colors?
cards.summary: With watercolors, a brush carries small bits of color mixed with water. A thin layer lets light reach the white paper and bounce back, so the paper helps the color look bright or pale.

cards.title: How do we know about the Shang dynasty?
cards.summary: The Shang dynasty ruled parts of northern China more than three thousand years ago. Its craftspeople made large bronze containers with carefully shaped patterns.

cards.title: How do wheat kernels turn into flour?
cards.summary: Wheat plants make dry kernels. A mill breaks the kernels into pieces and can sift the pieces by how big they are.

cards.title: How do written notes tell us what to play?
cards.summary: Written music gives performers a set of marks to follow. In a familiar kind of musical notation, notes sit on or between five lines called a staff.

cards.title: How do you feel rough and smooth things?
cards.summary: Try brushing a finger over paper, a sweater, or the top of a table. The push on the skin changes as your finger travels over tiny bumps.

cards.title: How do you find one point on a grid?
cards.summary: On a simple grid, start where the two number lines meet. The first number in an ordered pair tells you where to go sideways.

cards.title: How do you find the median?
cards.summary: Put the numbers 2, 6, 7, 10, and 50 in order from smallest to largest. The number in the middle is seven.

cards.title: How do you get to know a story character?
cards.summary: A character is a person, animal, or other being who takes part in a story. You can learn about one by watching what they do, hearing what they say, and noticing what other characters think about them.

cards.title: How do you measure area?
cards.summary: Area tells how much flat space a shape covers. Picture a rectangle made of square tiles that all have the same size.

cards.title: How do you measure around a shape?
cards.summary: The perimeter is the distance all the way around a flat shape. Picture a rectangular garden that is six steps long and four steps wide.

cards.title: How do you measure the space inside a box?
cards.summary: Volume tells you how much three-dimensional space something takes up. Imagine fitting small cubes into a rectangular box.

cards.title: How do you read the hands on a clock?
cards.summary: On many clocks, the short hand shows the hour and the long hand shows the minutes. When the long hand points at the twelve, it is at the start of an hour.

cards.title: How do you round a number?
cards.summary: Rounding replaces a number with a nearby number that is easier to say or use. To round 47 to the nearest ten, look at 40 and 50.

cards.title: How do you score in soccer?
cards.summary: In soccer, two teams try to get the ball into the other team’s goal. A goal counts when the whole ball goes over the goal line between the posts and under the crossbar, as long as the scoring team has not broken a rule.

cards.title: How do you smell something nearby?
cards.summary: A bowl of cut oranges can smell fresh from across a table. Some molecules leave the fruit and move through the air.

cards.title: How do your ears hear?
cards.summary: A sound sends vibrations through the air. When those vibrations reach your ear, they make a thin part called the eardrum move.

cards.title: How do your eyes help you see?
cards.summary: Light from the world enters your eye through a round opening. Clear parts near the front bend the light so it makes a sharp picture on a layer at the back.

cards.title: How do your fingernails grow?
cards.summary: Your fingernail grows from a group of cells under the skin near the base of the nail. These cells make new nail material that slowly pushes older nail forward.

cards.title: How does a bottlenose dolphin find a fish in murky water?
cards.summary: A bottlenose dolphin can see in the water, but it has another way to find food in poor light. It makes short clicks and listens for echoes that bounce back from nearby objects.

cards.title: How does a cacao seed become chocolate?
cards.summary: Making chocolate begins with cacao seeds surrounded by pulp. Changes during fermentation help develop the flavors.

cards.title: How does a database help find a record?
cards.summary: A database is an organized store of information that a program can look through. A class library’s database might store one record for every book.

cards.title: How does a flute make a sound without a reed?
cards.summary: A flute player blows a thin stream of air across an opening near one end. The air meets a sharp edge and sets the air inside the instrument moving back and forth.

cards.title: How does a giant anteater eat without teeth?
cards.summary: A giant anteater has a long, narrow face and no teeth. When it finds an ant or termite nest, it can rake open a small spot with its front claws.

cards.title: How does a giant manta ray eat tiny food?
cards.summary: A giant manta has wide fins that look like wings as it glides through the sea. Small flaps at the front of its head help guide water into its open mouth.

cards.title: How does a guitar change notes?
cards.summary: A guitar string makes a sound when you pluck it and it vibrates. On an acoustic guitar, those vibrations move into the body, which helps spread the sound.

cards.title: How does a hole become a natural rock arch?
cards.summary: In places such as Arches National Park, cracks split sandstone into long, narrow walls. Rain can get into cracks, and pieces of rock gradually break and fall away.

cards.title: How does a lever make a job easier?
cards.summary: A lever is a stiff piece that turns around a fixed point. A seesaw is a lever, and the support under its middle is the turning point, called a fulcrum.

cards.title: How does a number machine work?
cards.summary: A number machine is a way to picture a rule. Put in a number, follow the same rule each time, and see what number comes out.

cards.title: How does a pitcher plant catch insects?
cards.summary: Some pitcher plants make hollow leaves shaped like deep cups. An insect can slip inside and find it hard to climb out.

cards.title: How does a plant send sugar to its roots?
cards.summary: A leaf might make more sugar than it needs right away. The plant can send some of that sugar to other places through a tissue called phloem.

cards.title: How does a plant spread by underground stems?
cards.summary: A rhizome is a stem that grows sideways, often just below the ground. Roots can grow down from it.

cards.title: How does a protractor measure a turn?
cards.summary: A protractor is a tool with numbers marked around part of a circle. Put its center on the point where the two sides of an angle meet, and line its zero mark up with one side.

cards.title: How does a pulley help lift something?
cards.summary: A pulley is a wheel with a groove that guides a rope or cable. Hang one pulley from a support, run a rope over it, and tie a load to one end.

cards.title: How does a relay team pass a baton at speed?
cards.summary: In a track relay, each runner races part of the distance and hands a short baton to the next member of the team. The next runner may start moving before the baton arrives so both runners are going quickly during the handoff.

cards.title: How does a root know which way is down?
cards.summary: A root does not need to see the ground to grow down into it. Certain cells near many root tips can detect the direction of gravity.

cards.title: How does a router pass a message between networks?
cards.summary: A router joins networks and helps information travel between them. When a packet comes in, router equipment looks at where it is headed.

cards.title: How does a saguaro cactus save water?
cards.summary: A saguaro has a tall, green stem with folds along its sides. It can store water in that stem when rain is available.

cards.title: How does a script tell actors what to do?
cards.summary: A play script gives actors the words to speak and clues about what to do onstage. It may put each character’s name before their lines.

cards.title: How does a sea lion walk on a beach?
cards.summary: A California sea lion can turn its back flippers forward and use them to walk on land. That makes it easier to move around on a beach or a rocky shore.

cards.title: How does a search engine find pages?
cards.summary: A search engine can find pages ahead of time and build a list of clues about them. That list is often called an index.

cards.title: How does a seed wake up and grow?
cards.summary: A dry seed can hold a tiny plant and its food supply for a long time. When conditions fit what that kind of plant needs, the seed takes in water and swells.

cards.title: How does a strawberry plant make a runner?
cards.summary: A strawberry plant can stretch a long, thin stem across the soil. The stem is called a runner.

cards.title: How does a summer thunderstorm make ice?
cards.summary: A thunderstorm can send a strong stream of air upward. Water droplets often stay liquid even when they are below their usual freezing temperature.

cards.title: How does a team score runs in cricket?
cards.summary: Cricket has two ends of a long strip called the pitch. A batter stands near each end.

cards.title: How does a tennis rally work?
cards.summary: A tennis point starts with a serve. The player hits the ball toward the correct service box across the net.

cards.title: How does a trumpet make different notes?
cards.summary: A trumpet player presses their lips to a small mouthpiece and blows so the lips buzz. The air inside the trumpet moves with the buzz.

cards.title: How does a two-toed sloth live upside down?
cards.summary: A two-toed sloth can spend hours hanging from branches in a tropical forest. Its long, curved claws hook over a branch like handles, and strong limbs help hold it in place.

cards.title: How does a Venus flytrap catch a fly?
cards.summary: A Venus flytrap has hinged leaves with tiny hairs on their inside surfaces. When a small insect moves around and brushes the right hairs within a short time, a leaf can snap closed.

cards.title: How does a violin make a sound?
cards.summary: A violin player draws a bow across a string to make it vibrate. A small wooden bridge carries some of that motion into the body of the violin, which helps send sound into the room.

cards.title: How does a web address tell a browser what to open?
cards.summary: A web address is often called a URL. It can name a site and say which thing you want there.

cards.title: How does a woodcut make a picture?
cards.summary: To make a woodcut, an artist carves away the parts of a flat block that should stay blank on the picture. The raised parts that are left get covered with ink.

cards.title: How does American Sign Language work?
cards.summary: American Sign Language, or ASL, is a language that people can see. Signers use their hands, faces, and bodies to express ideas.

cards.title: How does an Asian elephant use its trunk?
cards.summary: An Asian elephant can pull a branch close, pick up a tiny object, and raise a load of water with the same tool: its trunk. A trunk is an extended nose and upper lip.

cards.title: How does an octopus fit into a narrow hole?
cards.summary: A giant Pacific octopus has eight strong arms with suckers and a soft body. The hard beak in the center of its arms is one of the widest hard parts it must fit through an opening.

cards.title: How does an orangutan move in a forest?
cards.summary: Orangutans spend much of their lives above the ground in the forests of Borneo and Sumatra. Their long arms help them reach for branches, and their hands and feet can hold on from different angles.

cards.title: How does barter work?
cards.summary: Barter means trading something directly for something else. You might trade a comic you have already read for a book a friend has finished.

cards.title: How does Boolean logic use true and false?
cards.summary: Some computer questions have two possible answers. A door is open or it is not.

cards.title: How does computer memory hold what you are using?
cards.summary: Think of your desk while you work. You may set out just the books and papers you need right now.

cards.title: How does cotton grow on a plant?
cards.summary: A cotton plant makes a dry fruit often called a boll. Inside that fruit, fine soft hairs grow from the surface of the seeds.

cards.title: How does erosion leave a narrow tower of stone?
cards.summary: A hoodoo is a tall, narrow shape made by rock wearing away unevenly. At Bryce Canyon, water enters cracks and can freeze when it gets cold.

cards.title: How does Hagia Sophia hold up its great dome?
cards.summary: Hagia Sophia is a historic building in Istanbul. Its builders had to fit a curved dome above a room with a square central space.

cards.title: How does liquid milk become solid cheese?
cards.summary: In many kinds of cheese making, a change in milk makes its proteins gather to form soft parts called curds. A watery liquid called whey can drain away.

cards.title: How does locking your device help protect it?
cards.summary: If you leave a tablet open, a person nearby may be able to read what you were doing or use an app that is already signed in. A device lock puts up a new check before letting someone get back to those things.

cards.title: How does moving your body help it work well?
cards.summary: When you move enough to breathe faster, your heart and lungs are moving more oxygen around your body. Over time, regular movement can help them do those jobs well.

cards.title: How does new seafloor form?
cards.summary: Long chains of underwater mountains rise along parts of the ocean floor. Many form where two plates move apart.

cards.title: How does one cell become two?
cards.summary: As you grow, the number of cells in your body goes up. One way it happens is that a cell copies its DNA and gets the two matching sets ready to move apart.

cards.title: How does soap help water wash away grease?
cards.summary: A greasy surface can make plain water form separate drops. Soap changes how these materials meet.

cards.title: How does soft clay become a hard bowl?
cards.summary: Potters can shape damp clay before it dries, when its small particles can move past one another. Drying takes out water and helps the shape hold.

cards.title: How does soft clay become a hard pot?
cards.summary: Wet clay can be pressed, rolled, or shaped as a wheel turns. A potter lets the finished shape dry before putting it into a special oven called a kiln.

cards.title: How does stainless steel resist rust?
cards.summary: Stainless steel has iron mixed with enough of a metal called chromium to make a very thin protective layer on its surface. That layer forms when chromium meets oxygen.

cards.title: How does stop-motion make objects look alive?
cards.summary: Set a toy on a table, take a picture, and move it a tiny bit. Take another picture and repeat.

cards.title: How does table tennis use the table in a rally?
cards.summary: A table tennis point starts when a player tosses a ball and strikes it so it bounces on their half of the table and then the other player’s half. After the serve, returns go directly toward the far side.

cards.title: How does tree sap become maple syrup?
cards.summary: In places with suitable weather, maple sap can flow well when nights are cold and days warm in late winter or spring. Sap from a sugar maple is usually clear and contains much more water than sugar.

cards.title: How does vitamin D help bones?
cards.summary: Vitamin D helps your gut take in calcium from food. Calcium is one of the materials your body uses to build strong bones and teeth.

cards.title: How does water reach the top of a tree?
cards.summary: When water leaves a tree’s leaves as vapor, it helps pull more water upward. Water molecules tend to cling to one another.

cards.title: How does weaving turn threads into cloth?
cards.summary: A weaver stretches one set of threads in order. Those threads are the warp.

cards.title: How does Wi-Fi connect a device without a cable?
cards.summary: Wi-Fi is one way for a device to join a nearby network. Instead of a cable to the device, it uses radio signals.

cards.title: How does wind build a hill out of sand?
cards.summary: Wind can bounce small sand grains along the ground. If the wind slows near a plant, rock, or other obstacle, loose grains can pile up.

cards.title: How does yeast make bread rise?
cards.summary: Bread yeast is a tiny living fungus. When it finds sugars available in dough, it can use them and release carbon dioxide gas.

cards.title: How does your blood plug a cut?
cards.summary: If a tiny vessel is damaged, its walls can squeeze inward to slow the flow. Small bits of cells called platelets stick to the broken spot and to each other.

cards.title: How does your body keep its balance?
cards.summary: Your brain checks several clues to see whether you are upright or tipping. Eyes can tell you how the room is moving in your view.

cards.title: How does your brain send messages?
cards.summary: Reaching for a pencil starts with messages traveling between nerve cells. A nerve cell is called a neuron.

cards.title: How does your brain talk to hormone glands?
cards.summary: A tiny gland under your brain is called the pituitary. A nearby part of your brain helps tell it what to release.

cards.title: How does your heart move blood?
cards.summary: Put a hand over your chest and you may feel your heart beating. Each beat is a squeeze from a muscle about the size of your fist.

cards.title: How does your rib cage protect you?
cards.summary: Your ribs curve around your chest like a long set of hoops. At the back they join the spine.

cards.title: How drinking water gets cleaned
cards.summary: Water from a river or lake can carry dirt and tiny living things. A treatment plant can add substances that help tiny bits of dirt clump together.

cards.title: How electric motors make things move
cards.summary: An electric motor makes a part turn. When electricity flows through a coil of wire, the wire makes a magnetic field.

cards.title: How electricity gets to your home
cards.summary: Power plants and other sources make electricity in many places. The power grid links these sources to towns, cities and buildings.

cards.title: How erosion carries rock and soil away
cards.summary: Erosion happens when water, wind, ice, or gravity moves soil and bits of rock. Rain can wash dirt from a path into a ditch.

cards.title: How escalator steps go flat at the top
cards.summary: An escalator runs a loop of steps around on a long chain. The visible steps ride upward or downward on wheels set in tracks.

cards.title: How far does sunlight reach into the ocean?
cards.summary: When you travel down through clear ocean water, the sunlight gets weaker. Near the top, enough light reaches plants and tiny algae for them to make food.

cards.title: How far is it around a circle?
cards.summary: Wrap a thread once around the outside of a flat round lid and measure the thread. That gives its circumference.

cards.title: How fiber optics guide a flash of light
cards.summary: A fiber-optic cable contains thin threads of glass or plastic. Light travels down a thread because its core and the layer around it bend light differently.

cards.title: How flowing water makes electricity
cards.summary: Water falling downhill can push blades around a wheel called a turbine. The turbine turns a generator, which sends electricity into wires.

cards.title: How gliders fly without an engine
cards.summary: A glider has wings but no engine to keep it moving forward. After a launch or a tow, the glider normally loses height as it moves through still air.

cards.title: How helicopters hover and turn
cards.summary: A helicopter’s main rotor spins long blades through the air. Each blade pushes air down and receives an upward push.

cards.title: How hurricanes get their strength
cards.summary: A hurricane is a large spinning storm that grows over warm ocean water. Warm, moist air rises from the sea.

cards.title: How Ingenuity flew in the thin air of Mars
cards.summary: The small helicopter Ingenuity rode to Mars under the Perseverance rover. The air on Mars is much thinner than on Earth, so there are fewer gas molecules for rotor blades to push against.

cards.title: How is a compound different from a mixture?
cards.summary: A compound forms when atoms of different elements join in a fixed pattern or proportion. Water is a compound.

cards.title: How is a sculpture different from a drawing?
cards.summary: A sculpture takes up space that you can measure in three directions: height, width, and depth. You might walk around a statue and see different details on each side.

cards.title: How is a sphere different from a circle?
cards.summary: A circle is flat, like the outline you draw around the bottom of a cup. A sphere is round in every direction, like a smooth ball.

cards.title: How large was a real Velociraptor?
cards.summary: Velociraptor was about as long as an adult human lying down, but much of that length was its tail. It was shorter and lighter than many movie raptors.

cards.title: How likely is something to happen?
cards.summary: Probability tells how likely an event is. A fair coin has two equally likely sides, so the chance it lands heads is one half.

cards.title: How lions live and hunt together
cards.summary: Lions often spend time in groups called prides. Females in a pride are often related, and they may care for cubs together.
