cards.title: How liquid can push up a heavy machine
cards.summary: When you squeeze liquid in a closed set of tubes, the extra pressure is passed to other connected parts. A small push on a narrow piston makes a pressure change that is passed to a wide piston.

cards.title: How living things change over generations
cards.summary: Living things often have small differences from others of the same kind. Suppose some beetles have a color that makes it harder for birds to spot them.

cards.title: How magnets pull and push
cards.summary: A magnet can pull some materials toward it without touching them. Iron is one example.

cards.title: How moving air and water carry heat
cards.summary: When a heater warms nearby air, that air often spreads out and becomes less dense. Cooler, denser air pushes it upward and moves into its place.

cards.title: How plants make their own food
cards.summary: A green plant uses sunlight, water, and a gas called carbon dioxide to make sugar. This is photosynthesis.

cards.title: How pollen travels from flower to flower
cards.summary: Flowers can make tiny grains called pollen. For many flowers to make seeds, pollen must reach a part of a flower that can receive it.

cards.title: How propellers push through air
cards.summary: Each blade of a spinning propeller acts like a small wing. Its slanted shape changes the pressure around it and pushes air backward.

cards.title: How quartz helps a clock count seconds
cards.summary: A quartz clock contains a little piece of a mineral that can vibrate. An electronic circuit gives the quartz small pushes so it vibrates at a regular rate.

cards.title: How railway signals help keep trains apart
cards.summary: One way to manage a railway is to divide it into sections called blocks. Equipment can tell a signaling system whether a train is in a block.

cards.title: How rainbows form
cards.summary: A rainbow can appear when sunlight shines into water drops in the air. The light bends on its way into a drop, bounces off the inside, and bends again as it leaves.

cards.title: How seeds start new plants
cards.summary: A seed holds the beginnings of a new plant. A coat helps protect the tiny plant inside.

cards.title: How ships use sound to map the seafloor
cards.summary: A ship can send a short sound into the water and wait for an echo from the bottom. Sound travels at a speed that researchers can estimate from the water’s conditions.

cards.title: How solar panels make electricity
cards.summary: A solar panel is made of smaller units called cells. When light reaches a cell, it can give energy to electrons inside the material.

cards.title: How sound moves through the air
cards.summary: Sound starts with something moving back and forth. When you pluck a guitar string, it shakes the air nearby.

cards.title: How spacecraft borrow speed from planets
cards.summary: Passing near a moving planet can change the path of a spacecraft. The planet’s gravity bends the spacecraft’s path as it flies past.

cards.title: How steam turned a locomotive’s wheels
cards.summary: A steam locomotive carries a boiler that heats water until it becomes steam. Pressure builds as the steam is kept inside.

cards.title: How submarines dive and rise
cards.summary: A submarine floats when water pushes upward as strongly as gravity pulls it downward. To dive, it lets seawater enter some tanks, replacing air.

cards.title: How sunlight warms Earth through empty space
cards.summary: The space between Earth and the Sun is mostly empty, so air cannot carry the Sun’s heat all the way here. Energy travels through space as radiation, including visible light and infrared light.

cards.title: How the northern and southern lights glow
cards.summary: An aurora can look like a glowing ribbon moving across a dark sky. Far above the ground, fast particles give energy to oxygen and nitrogen in Earth’s atmosphere.

cards.title: How the three main kinds of rock form
cards.summary: Scientists group rocks by the way they formed. Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens.

cards.title: How the Wright brothers learned to fly
cards.summary: Orville and Wilbur Wright tested gliders to learn how to balance an aircraft and turn it. They also made a wind tunnel to try different wing shapes before they built their powered Flyer.

cards.title: How tiny animals build coral reefs
cards.summary: A coral reef can look like a pile of rocks or plants, but it is built by small animals called coral polyps. Many kinds live in groups.

cards.title: How trains change tracks without steering
cards.summary: Train wheels follow metal rails, so a driver cannot turn a train the way a driver steers a car. At a junction, two short, tapered rails can move a little sideways.

cards.title: How was Ankylosaurus armored?
cards.summary: Ankylosaurus was a low, wide dinosaur that ate plants. Like the hard covering on a turtle, rows of bony plates helped protect it.

cards.title: How weather satellites watch moving storms
cards.summary: Weather satellites photograph Earth and measure kinds of light our eyes cannot see. A satellite high above the equator can go around once each day in the same direction as Earth turns.

cards.title: How wind turbines make electricity
cards.summary: A wind turbine turns moving air into electricity. When wind moves past the shaped blades, the difference in air pressure around them pushes them around.

cards.title: How wings hold up an airplane
cards.summary: A wing moving through air changes how the air moves over and under its surface. In flight, the wing pushes some air downward.

cards.title: Hungary
cards.summary: Most of Hungary is in a low basin surrounded by higher land in central Europe. The Danube divides Budapest, the capital, into parts that grew separately and are now connected by bridges.

cards.title: Iceland
cards.summary: Iceland is an island in the North Atlantic where very old ice and new volcanic rock can be found in the same country. Glaciers cover stretches of the interior, while heat close to the surface warms water underground.

cards.title: India
cards.summary: India is a country in southern Asia. The Himalayas rise along its north, and a large part of the country reaches south into the Indian Ocean region.

cards.title: Indonesia
cards.summary: Indonesia spreads along the equator on thousands of islands. Java contains Jakarta, one of the country’s largest cities and a major port.

cards.title: Io, Jupiter’s volcanic moon
cards.summary: Io is a moon of Jupiter with hundreds of volcanoes. Some send gas and dust high above its surface.

cards.title: Ireland
cards.summary: Ireland can mean an island in the Atlantic or the country that covers most of it. The country’s capital, Dublin, is on the east coast.

cards.title: Is a narwhal’s tusk a horn?
cards.summary: A narwhal’s long spiral tusk is a tooth that grows out through its upper lip. The tusk is seen most often on males.

cards.title: Is every square a rectangle?
cards.summary: To be a rectangle, a flat shape must have four straight sides and four right angles. A square has all of those things.

cards.title: Is ground fog really a cloud?
cards.summary: Fog is a cloud close enough to the ground for people to walk through it. On a quiet, clear night, the ground can lose heat.

cards.title: Is rhythm the same as the beat?
cards.summary: The beat is the steady pulse you can tap along to in much music. Rhythm is the pattern made by sounds and silences as time goes by.

cards.title: Is sea ice made from seawater?
cards.summary: Sea ice starts when ocean water becomes cold enough to freeze. Salt makes seawater freeze at a lower temperature than fresh water.

cards.title: Is the Web the same as the internet?
cards.summary: The Web is a huge collection of pages and other things that can get linked together. A browser gets a page from a place that can send it and lets you follow a link to another page.

cards.title: Italy
cards.summary: Italy reaches into the Mediterranean on a peninsula often compared with a boot. The Alps curve across the north, and the Apennine Mountains follow much of the length of the peninsula.

cards.title: Jamaica
cards.summary: Jamaica is an island in the Caribbean Sea south of Cuba. Its capital, Kingston, is on the southeast coast beside a large natural harbor.

cards.title: Japan
cards.summary: Japan is a chain of islands off the eastern side of Asia. A group of islands is called an archipelago.

cards.title: Jupiter, the biggest planet
cards.summary: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the biggest in our solar system. It is about eleven times as wide as Earth.

cards.title: Kazakhstan
cards.summary: Kazakhstan is a very large inland country with grasslands stretching across much of the north and desert and dry hills farther south. High mountains rise toward the southeast.

cards.title: Kenya
cards.summary: Kenya is in East Africa, and the equator runs across it. Its eastern coast meets the Indian Ocean.

cards.title: Kyrgyzstan
cards.summary: Mountains cover much of Kyrgyzstan, a landlocked country in Central Asia. Many belong to the Tian Shan range.

cards.title: Lake Baikal
cards.summary: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world. Looking at the thin shape it makes on a map gives little hint of how much water is below the surface.

cards.title: Laos
cards.summary: Laos is the only country in mainland Southeast Asia without a coast. Much of it is mountainous, but many settlements lie close to river valleys.

cards.title: Latvia
cards.summary: Latvia sits between Estonia and Lithuania on the eastern side of the Baltic Sea. Riga, the capital, stands near the mouth of the Daugava River on the Gulf of Riga.

cards.title: Lesotho
cards.summary: Lesotho is a country entirely surrounded by South Africa. It is unusually high: even the lowest places are more than a kilometer above sea level.

cards.title: Life aboard the International Space Station
cards.summary: The International Space Station is a science laboratory moving around Earth. Rockets carried its rooms and large pieces up one at a time.

cards.title: Life underground for naked mole-rats
cards.summary: A naked mole-rat lives in a network of tunnels beneath dry ground in eastern Africa. Its large front teeth stick out in front of its lips, so the animal can chew into dirt without filling its mouth with soil.

cards.title: Light and the colors we see
cards.summary: Light brings energy from one place to another. The Sun gives off light.

cards.title: Lithuania
cards.summary: Lithuania is the southernmost of the three Baltic states. Vilnius, the capital, is inland near the southeastern part of the country.

cards.title: Luxembourg
cards.summary: Luxembourg fits between Belgium, France, and Germany. The country and its capital city share the name Luxembourg.

cards.title: Madagascar
cards.summary: Madagascar is a large island off the southeast coast of Africa. Its high center contains Antananarivo, the capital.

cards.title: Malawi
cards.summary: Malawi is a narrow inland country in southeastern Africa. Lake Malawi follows much of its eastern side, and some shores rise quickly into hills and higher land.

cards.title: Malaysia
cards.summary: Malaysia has two main parts with a sea between them. One sits at the southern end of the Malay Peninsula, where Kuala Lumpur is the capital.

cards.title: Maldives
cards.summary: The Maldives are small, low islands in the Indian Ocean southwest of India and Sri Lanka. Many are part of rings of coral and sand around shallow water called atolls.

cards.title: Mali
cards.summary: Mali is a large inland country in western Africa with a desert north and generally wetter land toward the south. Bamako, the capital, stands beside the Niger River.

cards.title: Malta
cards.summary: Malta is a small country made up of islands in the Mediterranean Sea, south of Sicily. The two largest islands are Malta and Gozo.

cards.title: Mars, the red planet
cards.summary: Mars looks red from far away because its dust and rocks contain a kind of iron that has rusted. Up close, the ground can also look brown, tan, or gold.

cards.title: Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun
cards.summary: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system and the closest one to the Sun. Its rocky ground is covered in round dents called craters.

cards.title: Mexico
cards.summary: Mexico is in North America, just south of the United States. The Pacific Ocean is on one side and the Gulf of Mexico is on the other.

cards.title: Miranda’s cliffs and grooves
cards.summary: Miranda is one of the larger moons of Uranus, though it measures less than 500 kilometers across. Some parts of it have lots of round craters.

cards.title: Mongolia
cards.summary: Mongolia sits in inland Asia between Russia and China. The Gobi Desert takes up part of the south, while wide grasslands spread across much of the country.

cards.title: Morocco
cards.summary: Morocco is in northwestern Africa. The Atlantic Ocean meets the country on the west, and the Mediterranean meets it on the north.

cards.title: Mount Kilimanjaro
cards.summary: Mount Kilimanjaro rises from the plains of northern Tanzania to the highest point in Africa. It is made of several volcanoes joined together.

cards.title: Mozambique
cards.summary: Mozambique has a long coast on the Indian Ocean. The Zambezi River reaches the coast across the middle of the country, carrying water from far inland.

cards.title: Myanmar
cards.summary: Myanmar, also called Burma, runs from high mountains in the north to the coast of the Indian Ocean. The Ayeyarwady River flows south through much of the country, passing wide farming areas and spreading into a delta near the coast.

cards.title: Namibia
cards.summary: Namibia lies on the Atlantic coast of southwestern Africa. Near the sea, the Namib Desert contains stretches of gravel and huge sand dunes.

cards.title: Nepal
cards.summary: Nepal follows the southern slopes of the Himalayas between India and China. Along its southern side the ground is much lower and flatter.

cards.title: Neptune, the farthest planet
cards.summary: Neptune is the eighth planet from the Sun, so a trip around the Sun takes about 165 Earth years. It is cold at the tops of its clouds, and powerful winds sweep across them.

cards.title: Netherlands
cards.summary: The Netherlands lies on the North Sea, where several European rivers reach the coast. Much of the ground is low and flat.

cards.title: New Zealand
cards.summary: New Zealand lies in the southwestern Pacific Ocean and includes two main islands. A narrow passage called Cook Strait separates them.

cards.title: Nicaragua
cards.summary: Nicaragua’s west side has volcanoes and two large lakes close to the Pacific coast. Managua, the capital, is beside the smaller Lake Managua.

cards.title: Niger
cards.summary: Niger is a landlocked country in western Africa immediately north of Nigeria. A large share of its land lies in the Sahara, and dry country stretches far across the map.

cards.title: Nigeria
cards.summary: Nigeria reaches inland from the Gulf of Guinea in western Africa. The Niger and Benue rivers meet near the center, then flow south to a broad delta.

cards.title: Nile River
cards.summary: The Nile flows north through northeastern Africa to the Mediterranean. The Blue Nile carries water from Ethiopia, and the White Nile brings water from areas farther south.

cards.title: North Korea
cards.summary: North Korea occupies the northern part of the Korean Peninsula. Much of its land is hilly or mountainous, and broad lowlands are more common toward the west.

cards.title: Norway
cards.summary: Norway is a long, narrow country on the west side of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In many places the sea reaches inland between high rocky slopes.

cards.title: Our solar system
cards.summary: The solar system is our Sun and everything held in orbit by its gravity. That includes eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, and smaller objects such as asteroids and comets.

cards.title: Pakistan
cards.summary: Pakistan stretches from some of the world’s highest mountains in the north to the Arabian Sea in the south. The Indus River runs down through the country and brings water to many fields.

cards.title: Panama
cards.summary: Panama is a narrow country between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Its shape makes it part of the land bridge connecting Central and South America.

cards.title: Paraguay
cards.summary: The Paraguay River runs down through the country that shares its name. To the west lies part of the Gran Chaco, a broad landscape where many places are dry and hot.

cards.title: Perseverance, a robot geologist on Mars
cards.summary: Perseverance is a car-sized robot that landed in Jezero Crater in 2021. That place has a fan of rock left where a river once carried material into a lake.

cards.title: Peru
cards.summary: Peru runs along the Pacific coast of South America. Lima, the capital, is along the dry coastal strip.

cards.title: Philippines
cards.summary: The Philippines is a large group of islands in the western Pacific Ocean. Many maps group the islands into Luzon in the north, the Visayas in the middle, and Mindanao in the south.

cards.title: Phobos and Deimos, the moons of Mars
cards.summary: Phobos and Deimos are the two moons of Mars. They are both much smaller than Earth’s Moon and are shaped more like lumpy rocks than balls.

cards.title: Poland
cards.summary: Much of Poland is broad and low, with the Baltic Sea to the north and mountain ranges rising near its southern borders. Warsaw, the capital, stands beside the Vistula River.

cards.title: Portugal
cards.summary: Portugal looks mostly west toward the Atlantic Ocean. On land it borders Spain, and together the two countries cover most of the Iberian Peninsula.

cards.title: Romania
cards.summary: Romania stretches from the curve of the Carpathian Mountains to the Black Sea. Its capital, Bucharest, lies on lower land south of the mountains.

cards.title: Sahara Desert
cards.summary: The Sahara is a huge dry region that stretches across northern Africa from the Atlantic side toward the Red Sea. Its landscape includes flat rocky areas, mountains, patches of dunes, and places where water helps people and plants survive.

cards.title: Samoa
cards.summary: Samoa is an island country in the central South Pacific. Its two largest islands, Upolu and Savaiʻi, rose from volcanic activity.

cards.title: Saturn and its rings
cards.summary: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun. The wide rings around it are made of countless pieces of ice and rock.

cards.title: Senegal
cards.summary: Senegal lies on the Atlantic at the far western side of Africa. Dakar, the capital, stands on a peninsula poking into the ocean.

cards.title: Singapore
cards.summary: Singapore is a country built around a city on an island just off the tip of the Malay Peninsula. More small islands are part of it as well.

cards.title: Slovakia
cards.summary: Slovakia lies in central Europe, much of it in the Carpathian Mountains. The Tatras along the Polish border have some especially high peaks.

cards.title: Slovenia
cards.summary: Slovenia sits where parts of the Alps, the plains of central Europe, and the coast of the Adriatic come close together. Ljubljana, the capital, is inland.

cards.title: Solids, liquids, and gases
cards.summary: An ice cube, a puddle, and invisible water vapor are all made of water, but they act differently. In ice, the molecules stay in a pattern and jiggle around their spots.

cards.title: South Africa
cards.summary: South Africa occupies the southern edge of Africa, with shores on both the Atlantic and Indian oceans. Much of the inside lies high above the coast, and the land drops steeply on the way to the sea in many places.

cards.title: South Korea
cards.summary: South Korea occupies the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. Hills and mountains cover much of the land, with broader areas of flatter ground in the west and south.

cards.title: South Sudan
cards.summary: South Sudan sits inland in eastern Africa. The White Nile crosses the country from south to north and spreads through the Sudd, a vast wetland.

cards.title: Spain
cards.summary: Find the part of Europe that sticks down between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. Spain fills most of it, and Madrid, the capital, sits well inland.

cards.title: Sri Lanka
cards.summary: Sri Lanka is a large island just south of India in the Indian Ocean. Low coastal areas surround higher country in the middle of the island.

cards.title: Sudan
cards.summary: Sudan lies in northeastern Africa, south of Egypt and partly along the Red Sea. The Blue Nile and White Nile meet at Khartoum, the capital.

cards.title: Suriname
cards.summary: Suriname faces the Atlantic Ocean on the north side of South America. The capital, Paramaribo, is near the coast on the Suriname River.

cards.title: Sweden
cards.summary: Sweden fills much of the eastern side of the Scandinavian Peninsula. It borders Norway, and some of Sweden’s highest land is close to that border.

cards.title: Switzerland
cards.summary: Switzerland sits among mountains and lakes in central Europe. The Alps cover much of the south, and many towns sit on the flatter land farther north and west.

cards.title: Tajikistan
cards.summary: Tajikistan has much more mountain land than flat country. In the east, the Pamirs rise very high and hold glaciers that feed rivers.

cards.title: Tanzania
cards.summary: Tanzania stretches inland from the Indian Ocean across high country, lakes, and wide grasslands. Mount Kilimanjaro rises near the Kenyan border.

cards.title: Thailand
cards.summary: Thailand stands in mainland Southeast Asia and extends south down part of the Malay Peninsula. Its capital, Bangkok, grew beside the Chao Phraya River, whose low plain contains fields and many settlements.

cards.title: The Bahamas
cards.summary: The Bahamas are a chain of islands and low sandy islets in the Atlantic near Florida and Cuba. Many sit on underwater banks where the sea is shallow and can look pale blue from above.

cards.title: The Gambia
cards.summary: The Gambia is a long, narrow country in western Africa, with the Gambia River running through most of it. Senegal surrounds the land borders, and at its western end the river reaches the Atlantic Ocean.

cards.title: The Hubble Space Telescope
cards.summary: Hubble carries a polished mirror and cameras as it circles Earth. The mirror gathers light and brings it together so instruments can record very faint objects.

cards.title: The James Webb Space Telescope
cards.summary: Webb is a space telescope made to study infrared light. That light is invisible to our eyes, but Webb can record it.

cards.title: The kinds of light our eyes cannot see
cards.summary: Visible light is only a small part of a large family of waves. At one end, radio waves have much longer spaces between their peaks than visible light.

cards.title: The Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune
cards.summary: Beyond Neptune is a broad ring-shaped region called the Kuiper Belt. Countless bodies of ice and rock go around the Sun there.

cards.title: The Sun, our nearest star
cards.summary: The Sun is a star close enough to warm our planet and light up the daytime sky. Other stars can look like tiny dots because they are so far away.

cards.title: The water cycle
cards.summary: The same water can be in the ocean one day and in a cloud another day. Some water at the ocean’s surface changes into a gas and mixes with the air.

cards.title: Timor-Leste
cards.summary: Timor-Leste occupies the eastern half of the island of Timor and a smaller area on the western half surrounded on land by Indonesia. Dili, the capital, sits on the north coast with hills close behind it.

cards.title: Titan, a moon with lakes
cards.summary: Titan is Saturn’s biggest moon. It has a thick atmosphere made mostly of nitrogen.

cards.title: Tonga
cards.summary: Tonga is an island kingdom that stretches north and south through part of the South Pacific. Some islands are low and made mostly of rock built up by coral.

cards.title: Trinidad and Tobago
cards.summary: Trinidad and Tobago are two main islands at the southern end of the Caribbean. Trinidad, the larger island, lies just off Venezuela, across a narrow stretch of water.

cards.title: Triton, the moon that orbits backward
cards.summary: Triton, Neptune’s biggest moon, goes around Neptune in the opposite direction from the way the planet spins. This makes scientists think Neptune may have caught Triton after it had orbited the Sun on its own.

cards.title: Tunisia
cards.summary: Tunisia is a small country on the Mediterranean coast of North Africa. It stretches from hills and greener land in the north to salt lakes, dry plains, and parts of the Sahara in the south.

cards.title: Turkmenistan
cards.summary: Much of Turkmenistan is covered by the Karakum Desert. The country reaches the Caspian Sea to the west and has mountains along part of its southern edge.

cards.title: Tyrannosaurus rex
cards.summary: Tyrannosaurus rex was a large dinosaur that walked on two back legs. Some adults reached about 40 feet long.

cards.title: Uganda
cards.summary: Uganda is an inland country in eastern Africa. Part of Lake Victoria touches its southern side, and Kampala, the capital, is not far from the lake.

cards.title: United Kingdom
cards.summary: The United Kingdom brings four parts together: England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. The first three share the island called Great Britain.

cards.title: United States
cards.summary: The United States of America lies in North America and includes 50 states. Most form one connected group between Canada and Mexico.

cards.title: Uranus, the planet on its side
cards.summary: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. If Earth’s spin looks a bit like a tilted spinning top, the spin of Uranus looks more like that of a rolling wheel.

cards.title: Uruguay
cards.summary: Uruguay lies between Brazil and Argentina, on the side of South America that faces the Atlantic Ocean. Much of it is made up of gently rolling plains and low hills.

cards.title: Uzbekistan
cards.summary: Uzbekistan lies in Central Asia among deserts and river valleys. Tashkent, the capital, is in the east near higher ground.

cards.title: Venezuela
cards.summary: Venezuela has a Caribbean coast, a big river basin inland, and striking flat-topped mountains in the southeast. In parts of the interior, the Orinoco River flows past wide grassy plains called the Llanos.

cards.title: Venus, the hottest planet
cards.summary: Venus is the second planet from the Sun, almost the same size as Earth. Its air is mostly a gas called carbon dioxide.

cards.title: Victoria Falls
cards.summary: The Zambezi River spreads wide at the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe, then suddenly pours into a deep, narrow crack in the rock. The water hits with enough force to throw fine drops high above the cliffs.

cards.title: Vietnam
cards.summary: Vietnam follows the eastern coast of mainland Southeast Asia. Its shape is long and narrow in the middle and broader at both ends, where large rivers reach the sea.

cards.title: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2
cards.summary: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 left Earth in 1977 to study the outer planets. The spacecraft flew close enough to take detailed pictures without landing.

cards.title: Was Oviraptor really an egg thief?
cards.summary: When an Oviraptor skeleton was found on a nest, researchers first thought the animal had been trying to eat another dinosaur’s eggs. Its name means egg thief.

cards.title: Weather and climate are different
cards.summary: Weather is what the air outside is like now or over a short stretch of time. It might be windy this morning and sunny this afternoon.

cards.title: Were pterosaurs flying dinosaurs?
cards.summary: Pterosaurs were flying reptiles that lived while many dinosaurs walked on land. Their wings stretched between their bodies and one very long finger on each hand.

cards.title: What a tornado is
cards.summary: A tornado is a fast-spinning column of air that reaches from a storm to the ground. Tornadoes sometimes grow from large thunderstorms that are already turning.

cards.title: What are a humpback whale’s bubbles for?
cards.summary: Some humpback whales make loops of bubbles under schools of fish. The bubbles crowd the fish together as they rise.

cards.title: What are all the little bumps on broccoli?
cards.summary: The green head of broccoli holds a tight group of unopened flower buds. The small bumps you see are those buds gathered on branching stems.

cards.title: What are arteries and veins?
cards.summary: Blood takes a trip through tubes called blood vessels. An artery carries blood away from the heart.

cards.title: What are carbohydrates?
cards.summary: A potato, a pear, and a piece of bread can all provide carbohydrates. Some carbohydrates are sugars, such as the ones that help make a ripe pear sweet.

cards.title: What are factors?
cards.summary: Two numbers that multiply to make a whole number are a pair of factors of that number. For twelve, picture rows of buttons.

cards.title: What are mitochondria?
cards.summary: In many of your cells are small parts called mitochondria. They help turn energy from food into a form other parts of the cell can use.

cards.title: What are multiples?
cards.summary: Count by threes, starting at three. You get 3, 6, 9, 12, and so on.

cards.title: What are numbers below zero?
cards.summary: You can picture numbers on a line, with zero near the middle. Positive numbers are to the right, and negative numbers are to the left.

cards.title: What are pine cones for?
cards.summary: Pine trees make cones as part of making seeds. Small pollen cones release pollen into the air.

cards.title: What are pixels in a picture?
cards.summary: Many pictures on a computer are made of rows and columns of small spots called pixels. One part of the picture can contain darker pixels, while another contains lighter ones.

cards.title: What are plankton?
cards.summary: Plankton are living things that drift with moving water. Many are very small.

cards.title: What are the chimneys on the ocean floor?
cards.summary: In some places on the sea floor, water can enter cracks in the rock. It travels close to hot rock below, heats up, and returns carrying chemicals and minerals.

cards.title: What are the continents?
cards.summary: Continents are Earth’s biggest regions of land. A common way to name them uses seven: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America.

cards.title: What are the eyes on a potato?
cards.summary: The eyes on a potato are places where buds can grow. Each bud can start a shoot if the potato has suitable conditions.

cards.title: What are the little spears on an asparagus plant?
cards.summary: An asparagus spear is a young shoot that rises from a long-living part of the plant underground. People pick these shoots while they are still tender.

cards.title: What are the Moon’s dark patches?
cards.summary: The large dark patches you see on the Moon are plains made of solid rock. Long ago, huge impacts made low basins, and later lava filled some of them.

cards.title: What are the radius and diameter of a circle?
cards.summary: A circle is made of points all the same distance from a center. Draw a straight line from the center to the edge.

cards.title: What are the rocky ridges left by glaciers?
cards.summary: A glacier can carry pebbles, boulders, and sand in or on the ice. When its edge melts, the rock may stay behind, making a ridge called a moraine.

cards.title: What are the three branches of the U.S. government?
cards.summary: The United States divides federal government work among three branches. The legislative branch, Congress, makes federal laws.

cards.title: What are the tiny threads in cloth made from?
cards.summary: A cloth can contain thousands of tiny strands called fibers. Some come from plants, like cotton and flax.

cards.title: What are traits?
cards.summary: A trait is something you can notice or measure about a living thing. The color of a flower and a person’s height are examples.

cards.title: What are volleyball players trying to do?
cards.summary: Volleyball teams send a ball over a net and try to land it in the other team’s court. They can also score when the other team makes a mistake, such as hitting the ball out.

cards.title: What artificial satellites do
cards.summary: An artificial satellite is an object people built and put into orbit. Some satellites collect pictures showing where clouds are growing, where wildfires have spread or how much ice covers the ground.

cards.title: What barriers did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 address?
cards.summary: Even after the Constitution banned certain racial barriers to voting, officials in many places found ways to keep Black citizens from registering. Some required unfair tests or used confusing paperwork.

cards.title: What blows outward from the Sun?
cards.summary: The Sun’s very hot outer atmosphere sends a flow of tiny particles into space. This flow is called the solar wind, but it is not a wind made of ordinary air like the wind on Earth.

cards.title: What can a food label tell you?
cards.summary: Foods sold in many packages have a Nutrition Facts label. It lists certain materials in a stated amount of food, such as its fiber, protein, or iron.

cards.title: What can a loggerhead turtle crack with its jaws?
cards.summary: A loggerhead has a broad, heavy head with jaws strong enough to break the shells of animals such as crabs. The top of its shell is usually reddish brown.

cards.title: What can a portrait tell us?
cards.summary: A portrait is an artwork about a person or group of people. It could be a painting, a photograph, a drawing, or a sculpture.

cards.title: What can a town decide at a town meeting?
cards.summary: In some towns, a town meeting makes certain local decisions. People might talk about how much the town should spend or whether a town rule needs to change.

cards.title: What can a truth table show you?
cards.summary: A truth table is a chart for checking a logic rule. Suppose a sign responds to two buttons.

cards.title: What can fossil poop tell us?
cards.summary: A coprolite is a dropping that became a fossil. While an animal’s body tells us what the animal looked like, what it left behind may tell us something about how it lived.

cards.title: What can grow from a white oak acorn?
cards.summary: A white oak grows acorns, the hard nuts found under the tree. Much of an acorn gives food and protection to its seed while it waits.

cards.title: What can seven tangram pieces make?
cards.summary: A tangram is a set of seven flat pieces that can be arranged into a square. Moving the pieces apart gives you shapes to build new pictures.

cards.title: What can the buildings at Chichén Itzá tell us?
cards.summary: Chichén Itzá was a major city in the northern Yucatán region, in what is now Mexico. Builders raised a stepped temple often called El Castillo.

cards.title: What can you do if someone is mean online?
cards.summary: If someone keeps sending mean messages or puts up something cruel about you, show a grown-up you trust. You do not have to answer or try to fix it alone.

cards.title: What can you tell from the shape of a cloud?
cards.summary: Gray clouds that spread like a blanket are often stratus clouds. Cumulus clouds can grow in white heaps as air rises in separate columns.

cards.title: What causes the pulse you can feel?
cards.summary: Every time your heart sends blood out, the push makes a small wave of pressure travel through your arteries. You may notice that push as a beat in a place where an artery passes close to your skin, such as near your wrist.

cards.title: What changed for Japan during the Meiji Restoration?
cards.summary: In 1868, Japan’s government changed after centuries during which military rulers called shoguns had held much of its power. A new government ruled in the name of the emperor, whose reign was called Meiji.

cards.title: What changed in China during the Han dynasty?
cards.summary: The Han dynasty ruled for about four hundred years, with an interruption, after the Qin. Government officers kept written records and helped run provinces far from the main cities.

cards.title: What changes when a checker becomes a king?
cards.summary: In English draughts, often called checkers, each player starts with pieces on the dark squares of a board. An ordinary piece moves one square diagonally forward to an empty space.

cards.title: What could a Parasaurolophus crest do?
cards.summary: Parasaurolophus had a long hollow crest that swept back from the top of its head. The crest contained connected passages from its nose.

cards.title: What counts as personal information online?
cards.summary: Personal information includes details that can identify or locate you, such as your full name or where you live. Details that seem small, like the name on a team shirt, can become revealing when someone matches them with other clues.

cards.title: What did Abigail Adams ask lawmakers to remember?
cards.summary: Abigail Adams wrote letters to her husband John while he worked with other leaders of the American Revolution. In March 1776 she expected new rules to be written and asked him to consider women’s rights in those rules.

cards.title: What did an early little dinosaur look like?
cards.summary: Coelophysis was a lightly built dinosaur with a long neck and tail and small, sharp teeth. It walked and ran on its hind legs.

cards.title: What did Frida Kahlo put into her self-portraits?
cards.summary: Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter who often used herself as the person in a picture. She chose clothes, plants, objects, and settings that help tell the viewer something about her life and the ideas that mattered to her.

cards.title: What did George Washington do before and after independence?
cards.summary: George Washington was chosen to lead the Continental Army during the American Revolution. After the war, he led meetings at the Philadelphia convention that produced the United States Constitution.

cards.title: What did Mozart make with music?
cards.summary: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a composer from Salzburg, in what is now Austria. He began making and playing music when he was very young and traveled with his family to perform.

cards.title: What did people ask for at the Seneca Falls convention?
cards.summary: In 1848 a group gathered in Seneca Falls, New York, to talk about women’s rights. Organizers used language from the Declaration of Independence in a new statement.

cards.title: What did people build at Tikal?
cards.summary: Tikal was a large Maya city within the forest of what is now northern Guatemala. Its builders set steep temples and other large buildings around open squares.

cards.title: What did people do during the Viking Age?
cards.summary: During the Viking Age, people from parts of northern Europe traveled far by boat. Some raided towns, and others came to trade or settle.

cards.title: What did Protoceratops look like?
cards.summary: Protoceratops was a compact plant-eating dinosaur with a beak and a wide frill at the back of its head. It did not have the long horns of the later Triceratops.

cards.title: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 change?
cards.summary: People fighting unfair treatment in the United States had organized, protested, and gone to court for years. In 1964 Congress passed a law to ban certain kinds of discrimination.

cards.title: What did the Declaration of Independence say?
cards.summary: In 1776, the Continental Congress approved a document saying that 13 British colonies in North America were separating from Great Britain. The Declaration of Independence explained why they were taking that step and described rights they said people should have.

cards.title: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
cards.summary: President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863, during the Civil War. It declared enslaved people free in places it listed as still in rebellion against the United States.

cards.title: What did the Lewis and Clark expedition set out to learn?
cards.summary: Meriwether Lewis and William Clark led a group west in 1804. They traveled through country known to many Indigenous nations and kept notes about rivers, plants, animals, and people they met.

cards.title: What did the United States try to rebuild after the Civil War?
cards.summary: Reconstruction was the period when the United States tried to reunite after the Civil War and decide how freedom would work in daily life. New constitutional amendments ended slavery, defined citizenship, and addressed racial barriers to voting.

cards.title: What do captions do in a video?
cards.summary: Captions put words on a video near the time of the sound they explain. They can tell you what someone says and can also note important sounds.

cards.title: What do city streets tell us about the Indus civilization?
cards.summary: The Indus civilization grew in South Asia thousands of years ago. Today archaeologists study cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa to learn how people there lived.

cards.title: What do old buildings on an island in Tanzania reveal about trade?
cards.summary: Kilwa Kisiwani was a Swahili town on an island just off what is now Tanzania. Its people built homes, places of worship, and a palace using stone, including rock formed by coral.

cards.title: What do pH numbers tell us?
cards.summary: pH is a way to describe how acidic or basic a water-based liquid is. Around room temperature, pure water is neutral and has a pH about 7.

cards.title: What do plant roots do?
cards.summary: A plant’s roots reach into soil or another place where the plant grows. They help hold the plant steady when wind pushes on the leaves.

cards.title: What do state and local governments do?
cards.summary: In the United States, states make many rules for people and organizations within their state. Cities, towns, and counties may handle work that affects smaller places, such as collecting trash or taking care of local streets.

cards.title: What do the big numbers at the end of a runway mean?
cards.summary: A runway is a strip where an aircraft can take off and land. Large numbers at the ends usually describe the direction a plane faces as it goes along the strip.

cards.title: What do the stone walls at Great Zimbabwe tell us?
cards.summary: Great Zimbabwe was an important city in southern Africa several centuries ago. Skilled builders stacked carefully fitted stone in thick walls.

cards.title: What do the stripes on a barcode say?
cards.summary: A striped barcode uses dark bars and light gaps of different widths to represent numbers. A scanner can shine light on the stripes and measure the pattern that comes back.

cards.title: What do the walls of Mycenae tell us?
cards.summary: Mycenae was a wealthy center on the Greek mainland in the late Bronze Age. Builders used very large stones in its walls.

cards.title: What do white blood cells do?
cards.summary: White blood cells are part of your body’s defenses. There are several kinds with different jobs.

cards.title: What do your kidneys do?
cards.summary: Your kidneys help keep the right mix of water, salts, and other materials in your blood. Inside each kidney, tiny filters take some water and small materials out of blood.

cards.title: What does a computer processor do?
cards.summary: A processor is a chip that follows many simple instructions very quickly. One instruction might ask it to add two numbers.

cards.title: What does a fraction tell you?
cards.summary: A fraction can tell you how much of a whole you have. Cut a sandwich into four equal parts.

cards.title: What does a gallbladder do?
cards.summary: Your gallbladder is a little pouch tucked under your liver. As the liver makes bile, some of that liquid goes to the pouch and stays there between meals.

cards.title: What does a jury do in a trial?
cards.summary: A trial jury is a small group of people chosen to hear testimony and look at evidence in a court case. The judge tells them what legal rules to use.

cards.title: What does a number on plastic tell you?
cards.summary: Some containers have a small number surrounded by a three-sided shape. The number identifies a type of plastic material, which can help sorting.

cards.title: What does a QR code do?
cards.summary: A QR code is a kind of barcode with light and dark areas set out in a square. A camera and an app can look at the pattern and turn it into information.

cards.title: What does a variable do in a program?
cards.summary: A variable gives a program a name it can use when it needs a particular bit of information. A simple game might have a variable called score.

cards.title: What does a web browser do?
cards.summary: A browser is a program for opening and showing web pages. It uses the address you give it to ask another computer for material.

cards.title: What does a web server do?
cards.summary: A web server is equipment and software that can answer a request for web content. Suppose your browser asks for a school’s lunch menu.

cards.title: What does bone marrow do?
cards.summary: Deep inside some bones is soft material called marrow. Red marrow is a place where new blood cells are made.

cards.title: What does checkmate mean in chess?
cards.summary: In chess, a king is in check when one of the other player’s pieces attacks the square it is on. The player has to answer the threat.

cards.title: What does compressing a computer file do?
cards.summary: Computer files can take up less room if the information is stored in a shorter form. For example, a long string of twenty red spots might be stored as one note saying to draw twenty in a row.

cards.title: What does federalism mean in the United States?
cards.summary: Federalism means that governing power is divided between the national government and the states. The U.S.

cards.title: What does handwashing wash away?
cards.summary: A hand can look clean and still have material from things it touched. Some of that material clings to natural oils on the skin.

cards.title: What does it mean to become a citizen by naturalization?
cards.summary: A citizen is someone recognized as a member of a country under its laws. Some people are citizens at birth.

cards.title: What does it mean when a species is endangered?
cards.summary: An endangered species is one that is in danger of disappearing. If the last living member is gone, the species is extinct.

cards.title: What does NOT do to a logic value?
cards.summary: If a light is on, the sentence “the light is not on” is false. If the light is off, that sentence is true.

cards.title: What does pasteurized mean on a milk carton?
cards.summary: Pasteurizing milk means a dairy heats it for a carefully measured time and then cools it. The process reduces harmful germs so the milk is safer to drink.

cards.title: What does percent mean?
cards.summary: Percent means out of a hundred. Imagine a square marked with a hundred little boxes.

cards.title: What does privacy mean when you use a device?
cards.summary: Privacy is about how much other people can find out about you and who can see the things you share. Some games or apps let grown-ups choose whether a profile is seen by everyone or just by people they approve.

cards.title: What does serving size mean on a package?
cards.summary: The serving size on a Nutrition Facts label tells you how much food the numbers refer to. It might be a cup, several crackers, or another amount.

cards.title: What does sleep do for you?
cards.summary: When you sleep, you are less aware of the things around you, but your body and brain keep working. Your brain goes through several kinds of sleep in a repeating pattern.

cards.title: What does the biggest animal on Earth eat?
cards.summary: A blue whale can be longer than two school buses, but it mostly eats tiny animals called krill. To feed, it speeds into a patch of krill and opens its mouth wide.

cards.title: What does the decimal point show?
cards.summary: In 4.36, the decimal point sits between the ones place and the parts smaller than one. The 4 stands for four ones.

cards.title: What does the Fourteenth Amendment say about citizenship?
cards.summary: The Fourteenth Amendment says that people born or naturalized in the United States and under its authority are citizens. It also says states cannot take away certain rights without proper legal steps or deny anyone the equal protection of the laws.

cards.title: What does the mean tell you?
cards.summary: Imagine three friends have two, four, and twelve marbles. Altogether they have eighteen.

cards.title: What does the resolution of a picture mean?
cards.summary: One way to describe a digital picture’s resolution is to count how many pixels it has across and down. A larger count can hold smaller details when the picture was captured with those details in it.

cards.title: What does the thyroid do?
cards.summary: The thyroid is a small gland near the front of your neck. It makes hormones, which are messages that move in your blood.

cards.title: What does the U.S. National Archives keep?
cards.summary: The U.S. National Archives takes care of records made by the national government that have lasting value.

cards.title: What does the United States Supreme Court do?
cards.summary: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the federal court system. It reviews selected cases that raise important questions about federal law or the Constitution.

cards.title: What does the Universal Declaration of Human Rights say?
cards.summary: In 1948, representatives at the United Nations agreed on a statement about basic rights that people everywhere should have. It describes freedoms and protections that belong to people because they are human.

cards.title: What does vitamin C do?
cards.summary: Vitamin C helps your body make an important protein for skin and other tissues. It can also help your body take in iron from some plant foods.

cards.title: What does your body do with fat from food?
cards.summary: Fat is a kind of nutrient found in foods such as nuts, fish, and cooking oils. It can provide energy.

cards.title: What does your liver do?
cards.summary: Your liver sits mostly on the right side of your belly, beneath the ribs. Blood from much of your digestive system brings it materials from food.

cards.title: What does your skin do?
cards.summary: Skin forms a cover that helps keep water in your body and keeps many harmful things out. The surface can get scuffed, so new cells push up from below to replace old ones.

cards.title: What does your skull protect?
cards.summary: Your skull is made of several bones that fit together. Some form a strong case around your brain.

cards.title: What does your spine do?
cards.summary: Your spine is a column made mostly of individual bones called vertebrae. Many of them are separated by firm pads that cushion the bones and allow a little movement.

cards.title: What does zero do in a number?
cards.summary: Zero can tell you that there is none of something. An empty basket has zero apples.

cards.title: What energy can do
cards.summary: Energy lets things move or change. A rolling ball has energy because it is moving.

cards.title: What extra information can a file keep about itself?
cards.summary: A digital file can include details about the information it holds. A picture could keep a description of its size or the date it was made.

cards.title: What fossils tell us
cards.summary: A fossil is something from long-ago life that lasts into the present. It might be part of a shell or a tooth, or a mark left by a leaf or a walking animal.

cards.title: What fruit does chocolate start from?
cards.summary: Chocolate begins on a cacao tree, which grows in warm, wet places. Its fruits are thick pods with ridged sides.

cards.title: What gives the emperor tamarin its mustached look?
cards.summary: A bearded emperor tamarin is a small monkey with long white whiskers that curve away from its face. Groups move through trees in parts of the western Amazon, eating things like ripe fruit and insects.

cards.title: What goes on behind the scenes in a museum?
cards.summary: A museum collects and cares for objects that can teach people something. A museum might hold paintings, historic clothing, fossils, or dried plants.

cards.title: What happened at Lexington and Concord?
cards.summary: On April 19, 1775, British soldiers marched from Boston toward Concord to seize supplies the colonists had stored. Local people spread the warning.

cards.title: What happened at the ancient Olympic Games?
cards.summary: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia in Greece as part of a festival honoring the god Zeus. Athletes competed in events such as running, wrestling, and chariot racing.

cards.title: What happened on November 11, 1918?
cards.summary: By late 1918, the First World War had gone on for more than four years. Representatives of Germany and the countries fighting it agreed to an armistice, a promise to stop fighting under specific terms.

cards.title: What happened to most dinosaurs
cards.summary: About 66 million years ago, most kinds of dinosaurs disappeared. Scientists have strong evidence that a huge asteroid hit Earth at about that time.

cards.title: What happened when travelers arrived at Ellis Island?
cards.summary: Ellis Island was a large United States immigration station in New York Harbor. Some travelers arriving by ship went there to have their papers checked and answer questions.

cards.title: What happens in an inning of baseball?
cards.summary: In baseball, one team tries to score while the other plays in the field. A batter can send the ball into play and then try to reach first base.

cards.title: What happens inside a piano when you press a key?
cards.summary: Press a key on an acoustic piano and it moves a small hammer hidden inside. The hammer strikes one or more strings tuned for that note and quickly pulls away.

cards.title: What happens to ballots in an election?
cards.summary: Officials set up an election so eligible voters can choose among candidates or answer questions on a ballot. Depending on where they live, people might vote at a voting place or return a ballot by mail.

cards.title: What happens to old glass bottles in recycling?
cards.summary: A glass bottle can sometimes become part of a new bottle. At a recycling plant the old glass may be sorted, cleaned and crushed into small pieces.

cards.title: What happens to old leaves in the soil?
cards.summary: A leaf that falls into soil can become food for little animals, fungi and other living things. They break it into smaller parts.

cards.title: What happens when a river meets the sea?
cards.summary: Where a river reaches the sea, freshwater can meet water brought in by the tide. In many places the two meet in a partly enclosed area called an estuary.

cards.title: What happens when gears mesh
cards.summary: A gear has teeth arranged around its edge. When it touches another gear, each tooth fits in a gap and pushes the other gear around.

cards.title: What happens when lights share one path?
cards.summary: In a series circuit, the electric current has one path to follow. Imagine a wire from a small battery to a lamp, then to another lamp, then back to the battery.

cards.title: What happens when melted rock cools?
cards.summary: Melted rock below the ground is called magma. If it reaches the surface, it is called lava.

cards.title: What happens when the president vetoes a bill?
cards.summary: If a president disagrees with a bill passed by Congress, the president can send it back with objections. That is called a veto.

cards.title: What happens when two kinds of air meet?
cards.summary: A weather front is where a mass of colder air and a mass of warmer air meet. In a cold front, advancing cold air often slides under warm air, which can make the warm air rise quickly.

cards.title: What happens when two words become one idea?
cards.summary: A compound combines two words to name one thing or idea. A “snowman” is a figure made of snow, and a “notebook” is a book for notes.

cards.title: What helped Louisa May Alcott write Little Women?
cards.summary: Louisa May Alcott grew up with sisters in Massachusetts. She used parts of family life as inspiration when she wrote Little Women, the story of four sisters in a fictional family.

cards.title: What helped woolly mammoths live in the cold?
cards.summary: A woolly mammoth had a shaggy coat over much of its body. Smaller ears than many living elephants also helped reduce heat loss.

cards.title: What helps a tiger hide?
cards.summary: A tiger’s orange and black coat can be hard to make out in tall grass or in a forest with patches of sunlight and shade. Dark stripes break up the shape of its body.

cards.title: What holds the inside of a cell together?
cards.summary: The outer surface of a human cell is a very thin layer called its membrane. It separates the watery inside from the area around the cell.

cards.title: What is a cell in your body?
cards.summary: Your body is built from tiny living units called cells. Most are too small to see without a tool that makes them look bigger.

cards.title: What is a computer network?
cards.summary: A computer network links devices so they can send information to each other. For instance, a computer and a printer can share a link.

cards.title: What is a euro?
cards.summary: The euro is a kind of money used in many European countries, including France. A euro is divided into 100 cents.

cards.title: What is a file on a computer?
cards.summary: A file is a named group of stored information. A picture file may contain colors in a grid.

cards.title: What is a gene?
cards.summary: A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries information a cell can use. Many genes have directions for making a protein, such as one that forms part of a cell or helps it do a job.

cards.title: What is a genome?
cards.summary: The full collection of inherited instructions in a living thing is its genome. If you think of a gene as one passage in a big set of books, the genome is the full set.

cards.title: What is a haiku?
cards.summary: A haiku is a very short poem that began in Japan. It often makes you notice a small moment in nature.

cards.title: What is a landscape painting?
cards.summary: A landscape artwork shows a view of a place. It might show hills, a river, fields, or a busy town.

cards.title: What is a metaphor?
cards.summary: In a metaphor, an author talks about one thing as though it were something else. If someone writes “the moon was a silver coin,” they are comparing the moon’s look with a coin, not describing what the moon is made of.

cards.title: What is a nebula?
cards.summary: A nebula is a great cloud in space, made of gas, dust or both. Some clouds contain pockets where gravity draws material together until a new star can form.

cards.title: What is a pea pod holding?
cards.summary: A pea pod begins as part of a flower. It grows around several seeds, which are the round peas you may see lined up inside.

cards.title: What is a prime number?
cards.summary: Try arranging seven counters in a rectangle with no gaps. You can make one row of seven or seven rows of one, but you cannot make equal rows with both sides greater than one.

cards.title: What is a red tide?
cards.summary: Tiny algae are a normal part of the ocean. When some kinds get conditions that help them grow very quickly, they can form a big patch called a bloom.

cards.title: What is a second check when you sign in?
cards.summary: Some accounts check more than one kind of proof that the person signing in is allowed. After a password, a service may ask you to approve a message on a device that belongs to you.

cards.title: What is a simile?
cards.summary: A simile puts two unlike things side by side using a word such as “like” or “as.” If you write that a puddle is “as smooth as a mirror,” you help the reader see the water reflecting things around it. The puddle is still water.

cards.title: What is a still life in art?
cards.summary: A still life is an artwork about objects such as a bowl, a book, flowers, or fruit. An artist can put the objects close to one another so their shapes overlap, or spread them out so we notice each one.

cards.title: What is an algorithm?
cards.summary: An algorithm is a set of steps for solving a problem or doing a job. Imagine looking for your name in a list that is sorted from A to Z.

cards.title: What is an alphabet?
cards.summary: An alphabet is a set of letters used to write a language. In an alphabet, letters or groups of letters stand for sounds.

cards.title: What is an operating system?
cards.summary: An operating system is a set of programs that helps a computer run. It can give apps a way to open files, read keys, play sounds, or draw on the screen.

cards.title: What is blood made of?
cards.summary: Blood has a liquid part called plasma. It is mostly water and carries things such as dissolved nutrients and waste.

cards.title: What is cartilage?
cards.summary: Feel the end of your nose. It can bend a little without flopping.

cards.title: What is computer hardware?
cards.summary: A screen, a keyboard, and the pieces inside a laptop are all hardware. Hardware is the physical part of a computer.

cards.title: What is DNA?
cards.summary: Many of your cells hold a long, thin material called DNA. Its smaller parts can be thought of as four kinds of letters.

cards.title: What is fiber in food?
cards.summary: Fiber is material from plants that your body has trouble breaking down with its own digestive juices. You might eat some when you have an apple, oatmeal, or beans.

cards.title: What is hidden inside a tulip bulb?
cards.summary: A tulip bulb packs together a short stem, a new bud and thick layers that hold food. Most of this rests underground when the plant has no green top.

cards.title: What is inside a flower?
cards.summary: Colorful petals are the most obvious parts of many flowers. Look closer and you may see small structures that make pollen or collect it.

cards.title: What is latitude?
cards.summary: Latitude tells you how far north or south a place is from Earth’s equator. Imagine putting a belt around the middle of a globe.

cards.title: What is left over after division?
cards.summary: Think of giving seventeen markers to four people. Give each person one, then repeat as long as everyone can get another.

cards.title: What is longitude?
cards.summary: Longitude tells you how far east or west a place is from the line chosen as zero longitude. This starting line is called the prime meridian.

cards.title: What is phishing?
cards.summary: Phishing is a trick where someone makes a message look trustworthy to get you to give them something or do something. They might ask for a password, send a link that leads to a fake sign-in page, or try to get you to open a file.

cards.title: What is software?
cards.summary: If you can use one tablet to draw and then play a game, it is because different software runs on the same equipment. Software includes instructions that the computer can follow.

cards.title: What is the difference between lossy and lossless files?
cards.summary: If you make a story file smaller and later want every letter back, the method must save enough information to rebuild the whole thing. That is lossless compression.

cards.title: What is the Electoral College?
cards.summary: When people vote for president of the United States, their votes help decide which group of electors their state will pick. Those electors cast formal votes for president and vice president later.

cards.title: What is the internet?
cards.summary: The internet is a system that links many computer networks. Your device can send information to a nearby network, which has ways to reach others.

cards.title: What is the jet stream?
cards.summary: High above the ground, there are narrow bands of fast wind called jet streams. They often form near places where there is a large difference in temperature between masses of air.

cards.title: What is the Library of Congress?
cards.summary: The Library of Congress is a research library in Washington, D.C. It helps people in Congress find information they need and also makes materials available to the public.

cards.title: What is the nucleus of a cell?
cards.summary: Many of the cells in your body have a small part called the nucleus. It has its own border inside the cell.

cards.title: What is the tall sail on a Spinosaurus?
cards.summary: Spinosaurus had very tall bones projecting from its spine. Together they supported a sail-like rise above its back.

cards.title: What is the U.S. Bill of Rights?
cards.summary: The Bill of Rights is the name for the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution.

cards.title: What is the U.S. Congress?
cards.summary: Congress is the part of the United States government that makes federal laws. It has two parts, called the House of Representatives and the Senate.

cards.title: What is the U.S. Constitution?
cards.summary: The U.S. Constitution sets the basic rules for the United States government.

cards.title: What lived inside an ammonite shell?
cards.summary: Many ammonites left fossils that look like stone spirals. In life, an ammonite was a sea animal related to squids and octopuses, and the shell held its soft body.

cards.title: What made Uruk one of the earliest cities?
cards.summary: Uruk grew in southern Mesopotamia more than five thousand years ago. Thousands of people could live near one another there.

cards.title: What makes a can shaped like a cylinder?
cards.summary: A straight circular cylinder has two matching round ends and a curved surface between them. A typical soup can is close to that shape.

cards.title: What makes a cheetah such a fast runner?
cards.summary: A cheetah is built to run fast for a short stretch. Its legs are long and its back can bend and straighten as it runs.

cards.title: What makes a flat shape a polygon?
cards.summary: A polygon is a closed flat shape made by joining straight sides end to end. A triangle is a polygon with three sides.

cards.title: What makes a grain whole?
cards.summary: A grain kernel has an outer coat, a part that can start a new plant, and a large store of food for that plant. A whole grain keeps all three parts.

cards.title: What makes a kernel of popcorn burst open?
cards.summary: A popcorn kernel has a little water inside, a lot of starch, and a tough outer coat. Heat makes some of its water turn into steam.

cards.title: What makes a leatherback different from other sea turtles?
cards.summary: The leatherback is the largest kind of sea turtle. Its shell has long ridges and a flexible outer covering rather than the hard plates found on most other sea turtles.

cards.title: What makes a neon sign glow?
cards.summary: A real neon tube contains a small amount of neon gas. Electricity gives energy to atoms of that gas.

cards.title: What makes a number even or odd?
cards.summary: Put your socks into pairs. If each sock gets a partner, the number of socks is even.

cards.title: What makes a picture a collage?
cards.summary: A collage is made by arranging pieces of material on a surface and attaching them. The pieces might be colored paper, scraps of cloth, photographs, or something else.

cards.title: What makes a star explode as a supernova?
cards.summary: A supernova is an explosion that can make a star suddenly extremely bright. One kind happens when a very massive star’s center collapses and a blast sends much of the rest of the star outward.

cards.title: What makes a tsunami different from wind waves?
cards.summary: A tsunami starts when a great amount of ocean water is suddenly pushed out of place. An earthquake that lifts or drops part of the ocean floor can start one.

cards.title: What makes an angle wide or narrow?
cards.summary: An angle shows how far one direction turns from another. Open a book a little.

cards.title: What makes an ecosystem
cards.summary: An ecosystem includes living things in a place, the parts of the place that are not alive, and the ways they affect one another. Think of a pond.

cards.title: What makes fruit jam thick enough to spread?
cards.summary: A lot of fruits contain a substance called pectin. Under the right conditions, pectin molecules form a loose network that can hold water.

cards.title: What makes ice cream feel smooth instead of icy?
cards.summary: As ice cream freezes, some of its water forms solid ice crystals. A mixture with many tiny crystals can feel smooth on your tongue.

cards.title: What makes lightning and thunder
cards.summary: Inside a storm cloud, bits of ice can bump into each other and help separate electric charges. As the charges build up, electricity can suddenly move through the air.

cards.title: What makes little bumps rise on your skin?
cards.summary: You might see rows of little bumps on your arm in the cold, or while listening to exciting music. Each bump can happen when a tiny muscle tugs at a hair near its base.

cards.title: What makes ocean currents flow
cards.summary: An ocean current is water moving from one place to another. In shallow areas near the coast, the tide can make water flow into a bay and later flow out.

cards.title: What makes some twins identical?
cards.summary: Identical twins come from one fertilized egg that begins developing and divides into two groups of cells. This gives them almost the same DNA from the beginning.

cards.title: What makes something a chemical element
cards.summary: A chemical element is a kind of substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons. Every gold atom has 79 protons, so a very pure piece of gold has atoms of just one element.

cards.title: What makes something a mixture?
cards.summary: A bowl with rice and beans holds a mixture. You can add more of either food and still recognize the pieces.

cards.title: What makes the design of Angkor Wat unusual?
cards.summary: Angkor Wat is a large Khmer temple in Cambodia. A wide water-filled moat surrounds its grounds.

cards.title: What makes the wind blow?
cards.summary: Air pushes on things even when it looks empty. When air pushes more strongly in one place than in a nearby place, it starts moving from the higher pressure toward lower pressure.

cards.title: What makes two halves match?
cards.summary: Draw a heart, then imagine folding it down the middle. If every part of one half lands on the same part of the other half, the fold is a line of symmetry.

cards.title: What minerals are
cards.summary: A mineral is a solid that forms in nature and has a certain kind of material and pattern inside it. Quartz is one mineral.

cards.title: What part of a flax plant becomes linen?
cards.summary: A flax plant grows long groups of tough fibers inside its slender stems. After harvest, people loosen and remove other stem material so they can gather those fibers.

cards.title: What part of a fungus is a mushroom?
cards.summary: A mushroom can be the visible part of a fungus that makes and releases spores. Much of the same fungus may be growing as fine threads in soil, leaves or wood.

cards.title: What protects the outside of a tooth?
cards.summary: The part of a tooth that sticks above your gums wears a hard coat called enamel. It is tough enough to protect the tooth through lots of biting and chewing.

cards.title: What remains when a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers?
cards.summary: When a star close to the Sun’s size reaches its final stages, it can send its outer layers drifting away. The very dense center left behind is called a white dwarf.

cards.title: What rule means one or the other, but never both?
cards.summary: An imaginary sign might light up when only one person presses a button. If neither presses a button, it stays dark.

cards.title: What should you notice before sharing a photo?
cards.summary: A picture may show more than you meant to share. Look at the background.

cards.title: What shows that Norse travelers reached North America?
cards.summary: At L’Anse aux Meadows on Newfoundland, archaeologists found traces of buildings and objects made by Norse travelers. Turf once covered parts of the structures, helping people live in a windy coastal place.

cards.title: What tells a musician how fast to play?
cards.summary: Tempo is the speed of the beat in music. Imagine walking with a steady drum tap.

cards.title: What voting rule did the Fifteenth Amendment add?
cards.summary: The Fifteenth Amendment says the United States and states cannot deny or reduce voting rights on account of race, color, or having been enslaved. States approved it in 1870.

cards.title: What was a trilobite?
cards.summary: A trilobite was a small ocean animal related to today’s insects, spiders, and crabs. Its outer shell was divided along its length into a center section and two side sections.

cards.title: What was ancient Greece?
cards.summary: Ancient Greece included many communities around the sea. Some cities and the area around each city formed a separate government.

cards.title: What was apartheid in South Africa?
cards.summary: Apartheid was a system of laws in South Africa that separated people by race. It gave white people most political power and put limits on where many other people could live, travel, study, or work.

cards.title: What was Persepolis built to show?
cards.summary: Persepolis was a royal center in ancient Persia. Its builders made a huge level platform along a mountainside.

cards.title: What was the city at Cahokia Mounds like?
cards.summary: Cahokia was a large Indigenous city near the Mississippi River, in what is now Illinois. Its people carried loads of soil to make raised mounds.

cards.title: What was the city of Ur?
cards.summary: Ur was a large city in southern Mesopotamia. One of its best-known buildings was a ziggurat with stepped levels that rose above the flat ground.

cards.title: What was the Kingdom of Kush?
cards.summary: Kush was a kingdom farther up the Nile from Egypt, in what is now Sudan. People there built towns, temples, and burial places.

cards.title: What was the Louisiana Purchase?
cards.summary: In 1803, the United States bought France’s claim to a large stretch of land west of the Mississippi River. American leaders wanted a reliable place to send goods through New Orleans, a busy port near the river’s mouth.

cards.title: What was the thick dome on Pachycephalosaurus?
cards.summary: Pachycephalosaurus walked on two legs and had an unusually thick dome of bone on top of its skull. Smaller bony bumps surrounded part of the head.

cards.title: What was the Underground Railroad?
cards.summary: The Underground Railroad was a loose network of people, routes, and hiding places that helped enslaved people seeking freedom. Some people left on their own and received help along the way.

cards.title: What were Indus seals?
cards.summary: Archaeologists have found small carved seals at ancient Indus sites. A seal has a design that can be pressed into soft material, leaving a mark.

cards.title: What were oracle bones used for?
cards.summary: During the Shang dynasty, people at the royal court asked questions about what might happen. A question could be about rain, crops, or a trip.

cards.title: What were the three horns of Triceratops for?
cards.summary: Triceratops walked on four legs and ate plants. Two long horns rose above its eyes, and it had a smaller horn over its nose.

cards.title: What’s the difference between melody and harmony?
cards.summary: The melody is the line of notes you might hum when you remember a song. Harmony comes from notes sounding together or from the way groups of notes change underneath that tune.

cards.title: When does a new plant or animal become invasive?
cards.summary: Some living things reach new places when people carry boats, plants, soil, or other goods between regions. Some newcomers never establish a wild population.

cards.title: When does an AND rule say yes?
cards.summary: Imagine a pretend treasure chest that opens only when you have a key and stand on a marked square. You need both parts.

cards.title: When does an OR rule say yes?
cards.summary: Suppose a pretend gate opens if you have a round token or a square token. With either token the gate opens.

cards.title: Where an echo comes from
cards.summary: An echo is a sound you hear after it bounces off a surface and returns. At the edge of a canyon, a shout can travel to a cliff and back.

cards.title: Where are we in the Milky Way?
cards.summary: The Sun is one star in a huge disk of stars called the Milky Way. If you could look down on that disk from well above it, you would see a long bar of stars in the middle and spiral arms curving around it.

cards.title: Where did corn come from?
cards.summary: Corn, also called maize, grew into a farm crop from a wild plant called teosinte. This change began thousands of years ago in what is now Mexico.

cards.title: Where did the Winnie-the-Pooh characters come from?
cards.summary: English writer A. A.

cards.title: Where did Zheng He’s fleets travel?
cards.summary: In the early 1400s, the rulers of Ming China sent fleets of ships across the Indian Ocean. A leader named Zheng He commanded several of these journeys.

cards.title: Where does a battery get its energy?
cards.summary: A battery contains materials that can react with each other. You can connect the two ends into a circuit so the reaction helps move electrons around the outside path.

cards.title: Where does food go after you swallow it?
cards.summary: Digestion begins before you swallow. Your teeth break up food, and saliva starts breaking down some of it.

cards.title: Where does hair grow from?
cards.summary: A hair gets longer from the end hidden inside the skin. That end sits in a small pocket called a follicle.

cards.title: Where does rain on a street go?
cards.summary: After rain falls on a street, much of it cannot soak through the hard surface. Water runs along slopes and gutters to an opening or grate.

cards.title: Where does sugar go when it dissolves?
cards.summary: When sugar dissolves, it is still there even after you stop seeing the grains. Water separates the sugar molecules from the grain and surrounds them without breaking apart the individual molecules.

cards.title: Where does vanilla flavor come from?
cards.summary: Vanilla can come from the fruit of a climbing orchid. People often call the long fruit a vanilla bean, even though it is an orchid pod.

cards.title: Where is most of a fungus hiding?
cards.summary: A fungus often grows as a net of tiny branching threads. The whole net is called mycelium.

cards.title: Where is the deepest part of the ocean?
cards.summary: The ocean floor is not flat. Long, narrow valleys called trenches cut deeply below nearby areas.

cards.title: Where is the equator?
cards.summary: The equator is an imaginary circle around Earth halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. It divides Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and Southern Hemisphere.

cards.title: Where on a pumpkin vine does a pumpkin begin?
cards.summary: A pumpkin vine sends its stems across the ground. It can make flowers that release pollen and other flowers where fruits can start.

cards.title: Where very long-traveling comets may come from
cards.summary: Some comets pass the Sun once and may take thousands of years to return. Scientists think many begin in a vast outer region called the Oort Cloud.

cards.title: Where water goes after it runs down the drain
