cards.summary: Water that leaves sinks or toilets can move through sewer pipes to a treatment plant. Screens catch big pieces of trash first.

cards.title: Which cave formations hang down and which grow up?
cards.summary: Water can pass through rock and carry dissolved material into a cave. As a drop hangs from the ceiling, it may leave a little solid mineral.

cards.title: Which part of a calculation comes first?
cards.summary: If you see 2 + 3 × 4, you might think to add first. In the usual order of operations, multiplication comes before addition, so three times four is twelve and the total is fourteen.

cards.title: Which part of a carrot plant do we eat?
cards.summary: The familiar part of a carrot is a thick main root. It can hold food the plant made earlier in its green leaves.

cards.title: Which pieces of space rock reach the ground?
cards.summary: Many bits of space rock heat up during their fast trip into Earth’s air. They can make a streak of light called a meteor.

cards.title: Which shapes can tile a floor without leaving gaps?
cards.summary: A tessellation covers a flat surface with shapes that fit just up to one another, without gaps or overlaps. Squares can do it because four square corners meet exactly around one point.

cards.title: Who built the large palaces of ancient Crete?
cards.summary: The people we call Minoans lived on Crete thousands of years ago. They built large groups of rooms around open courts at places such as Knossos.

cards.title: Who tells a story?
cards.summary: The narrator is the voice that tells the story. A storyteller who says “I opened the door” can tell you what it felt like to be there.

cards.title: Who wrote The Wonderful Wizard of Oz?
cards.summary: L. Frank Baum wrote a story about Dorothy, a girl who travels from Kansas to the made-up Land of Oz.

cards.title: Why a clear daytime sky looks blue
cards.summary: Sunlight contains many colors. As it passes through the atmosphere, tiny molecules of gas send some of its light in new directions.

cards.title: Why a push comes with a push back
cards.summary: If you push your hands against a wall, the wall pushes back on your hands just as hard. Every push or pull between two objects works in both directions.

cards.title: Why a ramp makes lifting easier
cards.summary: A ramp gives you a longer path to a higher place. If you lifted a box straight up, you would have to support its full weight while lifting.

cards.title: Why a screw moves forward when turned
cards.summary: A screw has a spiral ridge called a thread around it. Turning the screw is like moving along a ramp that has been wrapped around a rod.

cards.title: Why a seat belt makes stopping safer
cards.summary: When a moving car slows suddenly, the people inside are still moving forward until a force slows them too. A seat belt connects the rider to the vehicle so they slow down along with the car.

cards.title: Why a spacecraft flew through the Sun’s outer atmosphere
cards.summary: The Parker Solar Probe was built to study the Sun from closer than any earlier spacecraft. Its wide heat shield stays pointed toward the Sun, keeping much of the direct radiation off the instruments behind it.

cards.title: Why a spoon handle gets warm
cards.summary: Put a metal spoon in something warm and, after a while, you may feel the handle warm up too. The warm end gives energy to nearby parts of the metal.

cards.title: Why airplanes change the shape of their wings
cards.summary: If you look out at a plane’s wing near landing, parts along the back may slide out or tilt down. These parts are called flaps.

cards.title: Why airports have traffic control towers
cards.summary: Many airports have tall towers where controllers can look out at the runways and paths between gates. They talk with pilots and help keep aircraft apart while airplanes land, take off or move on the ground.

cards.title: Why are beans useful in meals?
cards.summary: Many of the beans people eat are seeds that grow in pods. Peas and lentils come from related plants.

cards.title: Why are coast redwoods famous?
cards.summary: Coast redwoods are the tallest living trees known. They grow naturally along a narrow stretch of the Pacific coast in California and a small part of Oregon.

cards.title: Why are coffee beans taken from cherries?
cards.summary: A coffee plant grows small fruits around seeds. People call the ripe fruits coffee cherries because many look rounded and red, like cherries.

cards.title: Why are raisins smaller than grapes?
cards.summary: A grape carries a lot of water inside it. When it is dried into a raisin, much of that water leaves and the skin wrinkles around the smaller fruit.

cards.title: Why are some volcanic islands lined up?
cards.summary: A hot spot can supply melted rock beneath a moving plate. A volcano may grow above the hot spot until it reaches the ocean surface and makes an island.

cards.title: Why are there clay soldiers near an emperor’s tomb?
cards.summary: The First Emperor of Qin had a huge burial site built near what is now Xi’an. People shaped and fired clay figures of soldiers, horses, and other members of his court.

cards.title: Why are there different swimming strokes?
cards.summary: In swimming, a stroke is a pattern of arm and leg movements that moves a swimmer through water. In front crawl, the arms take turns reaching and pulling.

cards.title: Why are there rows of trees along some fields?
cards.summary: A strong wind can carry loose soil off an open field. Rows of trees or shrubs can slow some of the air moving near the ground on the sheltered side.

cards.title: Why be careful with messages from people you just met online?
cards.summary: When you meet someone through a game, you may know their character name and how they play. You may know very little about who they are away from the game.

cards.title: Why bicycles have different gears
cards.summary: A bicycle chain moves between toothed wheels called sprockets. A low gear makes your feet turn the pedals more times for each turn of the rear wheel.

cards.title: Why birds are living dinosaurs
cards.summary: Birds belong to one branch of the dinosaur family. Their early relatives were small, two-legged dinosaurs that lived long before people.

cards.title: Why brakes press against a spinning wheel
cards.summary: In many cars, pressing the brake pedal pushes liquid through narrow tubes or controls a system that does. At a wheel, the pressure makes brake pads press on a spinning metal disc.

cards.title: Why bridge frames are full of triangles
cards.summary: A rectangular frame can lean sideways if its joints are free to turn. Add a diagonal bar, and you split the frame into two triangles.

cards.title: Why build a circle where roads meet?
cards.summary: A modern roundabout sends traffic around a small island so paths join in the same direction. The road bends as it leads toward the center, which helps drivers slow before entering the circle.

cards.title: Why can a beluga turn its head?
cards.summary: Belugas live in Arctic and nearby waters. A young beluga is gray, and most become white as they grow older.

cards.title: Why can a rubbed balloon stick to a wall?
cards.summary: Rub a balloon against some fabrics and a few electrons can move from one surface to the other. That leaves one surface with extra negative charge and the other with less.

cards.title: Why can a vector picture grow without getting blocky?
cards.summary: A vector picture can describe a shape by saying where its edges and curves go. A drawing of a blue circle can be saved as the circle’s center, its size, and its color.

cards.title: Why can an onion make your eyes water?
cards.summary: A knife breaks many onion cells when it slices through their layers. Materials kept apart in an uncut onion can then mix.

cards.title: Why can baking soda make batter rise?
cards.summary: Baking soda can react with a food acid in wet batter and release carbon dioxide gas. The gas makes little bubbles that take up room.

cards.title: Why can falling rain turn to ice on a branch?
cards.summary: Freezing rain begins with liquid drops. Those drops can cool below water’s usual freezing point without turning solid right away.

cards.title: Why can lichens grow on bare rocks?
cards.summary: A lichen grows when a fungus lives closely with a partner that can make sugars using light. That partner can be a kind of alga or a kind of tiny living thing called a cyanobacterium.

cards.title: Why can people still see streets and houses at Pompeii?
cards.summary: Pompeii was a town near Mount Vesuvius in what is now Italy. In 79 CE the volcano erupted, and ash and other material covered the town.

cards.title: Why can plastics feel so different?
cards.summary: A lot of the material in plastic is made from very long molecules. Such molecules may form loose chains or a tighter network.

cards.title: Why can salt melt ice on a road?
cards.summary: Ordinary water can freeze at a certain temperature, but water with dissolved salt in it can stay liquid below that temperature. Salt on an icy road can dissolve in small amounts of liquid water at the surface and form salty water.

cards.title: Why can soap make a bubble last?
cards.summary: A bubble forms when air stretches a thin liquid film around itself. Water alone usually cannot keep that delicate film from breaking for very long.

cards.title: Why can the ground suddenly sink into a hole?
cards.summary: Rainwater can slowly dissolve some kinds of rock underground, including limestone. The openings can grow as more water passes through.

cards.title: Why can water flow straight out of a hillside?
cards.summary: A spring is a place where underground water reaches the surface. Rain or melted snow can sink through gaps in soil and rock.

cards.title: Why can water rush away from a beach?
cards.summary: As waves break near a beach, they push water toward land. Some of that water flows back out in a narrow, fast-moving stream called a rip current.

cards.title: Why can you see several colors in one piece of granite?
cards.summary: A polished piece of granite can show pink, white, gray, or dark grains that fit together. The grains are different minerals.

cards.title: Why can your body react before you decide?
cards.summary: Pulling your hand away from a hot surface can happen before you have time to plan to move. Nerves on the skin send a message inward.

cards.title: Why can your shoulder move in so many directions?
cards.summary: At your shoulder, the rounded top of your upper arm bone fits into a socket. Imagine a ball resting in a shallow cup.

cards.title: Why comets grow tails
cards.summary: A comet is a small body of ice, dust, and rock that travels around the Sun. When a comet comes into warmer parts of the solar system, some of its ice changes straight into gas.

cards.title: Why dark spots appear on the Sun
cards.summary: Some parts of the Sun are held by strong magnetic fields. Those fields can reduce the motion that normally carries heat up from below.

cards.title: Why did ancient Romans build so many roads?
cards.summary: Roads tied ancient Rome to places across its growing territory. A good road made it easier to move travelers, soldiers, animals, and goods over land.

cards.title: Why did builders carve buildings into cliffs at Petra?
cards.summary: Petra was a trading city of the Nabataeans in what is now Jordan. Tall sandstone cliffs surrounded it.

cards.title: Why did cities grow between the Tigris and Euphrates?
cards.summary: Mesopotamia was a region around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. In its drier southern lands, people dug channels to bring river water to their fields.

cards.title: Why did Constantinople become an important city?
cards.summary: Constantinople stood beside the Bosporus, a narrow waterway connecting larger seas between Europe and Asia. That position brought ships and trade near the city.

cards.title: Why did countries create the League of Nations?
cards.summary: After the First World War, leaders wanted countries to have a place to talk through disagreements before turning to fighting. The League of Nations began in 1920, with its center in Geneva, Switzerland.

cards.title: Why did countries form the United Nations?
cards.summary: Near the end of the Second World War, delegates from many countries came to San Francisco. They wrote a charter for an organization called the United Nations.

cards.title: Why did delegates meet in Philadelphia in 1787?
cards.summary: After independence, the United States had a national government with limited power. Representatives met in Philadelphia in 1787 to consider changes.

cards.title: Why did Diplodocus have such a long tail?
cards.summary: Diplodocus was a long-necked dinosaur with a tail that narrowed to a thin tip. The tail alone made up a large part of its length.

cards.title: Why did Iguanodon have a spike on its thumb?
cards.summary: One finger on an Iguanodon hand ended in an unusual spike. Some early researchers put the spike on the dinosaur’s nose because they had only scattered fossils to work with.

cards.title: Why did Jacob Lawrence tell one history in many paintings?
cards.summary: Jacob Lawrence painted a series about the movement of many Black Americans from the South to other regions of the United States. One picture can show a train station, another a room, another a group waiting for work.

cards.title: Why did Jules Verne write about imagined trips?
cards.summary: French writer Jules Verne told stories about journeys across oceans, around the world, and to places nobody could really visit. In one book travelers ride in an imagined submarine.

cards.title: Why did Lincoln give a short speech at Gettysburg?
cards.summary: In November 1863, people gathered in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, to open a cemetery for soldiers who had fought there. After a long speech by another speaker, President Abraham Lincoln spoke briefly.

cards.title: Why did Mansa Musa travel across Africa?
cards.summary: Mansa Musa was a ruler of the Mali Empire. In the 1300s he went on pilgrimage to Mecca, a city important to Muslims.

cards.title: Why did Maya people use more than one calendar?
cards.summary: Maya people kept track of several cycles of time. One calendar counted 365 days.

cards.title: Why did more people begin working in factories?
cards.summary: For a long time, people could spin thread or weave cloth in homes and small workshops. In Britain, larger machines made it possible to gather several parts of this work in one place.

cards.title: Why did people build the Great Wall of China?
cards.summary: Rulers in different periods built walls, gates, and towers along parts of China’s northern frontier. Walls could slow a raid and guide people toward guarded crossings.

cards.title: Why did people dig a canal across part of Egypt?
cards.summary: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea through Egypt. A ship traveling between parts of Europe and Asia can use it rather than going all the way around southern Africa.

cards.title: Why did people press signs into clay?
cards.summary: In ancient Mesopotamia, people used clay tablets as writing surfaces. A writer used a tool called a stylus to press small wedge shapes into soft clay.

cards.title: Why did protesters dump tea into Boston Harbor?
cards.summary: In 1773, Britain gave one company new ways to sell tea in its American colonies. A tax on the tea still applied.

cards.title: Why did Stegosaurus have plates down its back?
cards.summary: Two rows of tall plates stood along the back of Stegosaurus. The plates were made of bone, but sat in the skin rather than joining the backbone.

cards.title: Why did the Brothers Grimm collect fairy tales?
cards.summary: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected stories in German-speaking Europe and printed versions of many of them. Tales people tell aloud can change a little with each storyteller.

cards.title: Why did the Supreme Court rule against separate public schools?
cards.summary: In several places, families challenged rules that sent Black and white children to separate public schools. The Supreme Court considered the cases together under the name Brown v.

cards.title: Why did the United States fight a Civil War?
cards.summary: In 1861, a group of Southern states tried to leave the United States and formed the Confederacy. Their leaders wanted to protect slavery, a system that kept people forced to work as property.

cards.title: Why did Timbuktu become a center for books?
cards.summary: Timbuktu grew near a point where desert travelers could connect with routes into West Africa. Markets brought people to the town, and scholars came to teach and study.

cards.title: Why did travelers come to the Tang capital?
cards.summary: During the Tang dynasty, Chang’an was a large capital with ordered streets and busy markets. Officials, traders, and travelers arrived from far apart places.

cards.title: Why did Van Gogh paint several sunflower pictures?
cards.summary: Vincent van Gogh made several paintings of sunflowers in jars and vases. Some use lots of yellow, yet the light and dark yellows still let you pick out the petals, flower heads, and background.

cards.title: Why did wolves return to Yellowstone?
cards.summary: Gray wolves once lived in Yellowstone, but people removed them from the park and few remained nearby. In the 1990s, wildlife workers brought wolves from Canada back to the area.

cards.title: Why do apple growers join pieces of two trees?
cards.summary: A seed from a favorite apple can grow a tree, but the young tree may make apples with different qualities. Growers often attach a piece from a known apple tree to the roots and lower stem of another one.

cards.title: Why do astronauts float in orbit?
cards.summary: Earth’s gravity pulls on an orbiting astronaut and the spacecraft around them. Both are falling toward Earth, but both are traveling sideways so fast that Earth’s curved surface keeps dropping away beneath them.

cards.title: Why do blueberry bushes like acidic soil?
cards.summary: Different plants grow best in different kinds of soil. Many blueberries do well in soil that is more acidic than the soil preferred by a lot of other garden crops.

cards.title: Why do brown rice and white rice look different?
cards.summary: A rice grain grows inside a hard covering called a hull. A machine takes that outside covering off before the rice is eaten.

cards.title: Why do children lose their first teeth?
cards.summary: A child’s first set of teeth fits into a small jaw. As the jaw grows, many of these teeth have to make room for a later set.

cards.title: Why do computers send messages in little packets?
cards.summary: A long message can share a busy route more easily if it travels as little pieces called packets. Think of mailing a long story as a series of postcards.

cards.title: Why do computers use 0s and 1s?
cards.summary: A computer can store a tiny piece of information in one of two states. We give those states the names 0 and 1.

cards.title: Why do crystals have neat shapes?
cards.summary: In a crystal, very small particles fit together in a pattern that repeats. Adding more particles in matching positions can grow that same pattern outward.

cards.title: Why do different parts of the US government check one another?
cards.summary: The Constitution gives different kinds of work to Congress, the president, and the courts. It also gives one branch ways to limit or review actions taken by another.

cards.title: Why do distant objects look smaller in pictures?
cards.summary: Stand at one end of a long hallway. The walls get closer together in your view as they get farther away.

cards.title: Why do fables often use talking animals?
cards.summary: A fable is a short story that suggests a lesson. A small mouse in an old fable helps a much larger lion, showing that size does not decide who can be helpful.

cards.title: Why do farmers change crops in a field?
cards.summary: Crop rotation means planning to grow different crops in the same place at different times. If a disease can easily spread among one kind of plant, growing an unrelated plant in that field for a while can leave the disease with fewer plants to infect.

cards.title: Why do flat maps stretch Earth?
cards.summary: The surface of Earth curves, but paper is flat. Any way of drawing that curved surface on a flat page changes something about the places on it.

cards.title: Why do gardeners cover soil with mulch?
cards.summary: A layer of straw, leaves or small wood chips can keep sun and wind from touching bare soil directly. This covering is called mulch.

cards.title: Why do giant pandas eat so much bamboo?
cards.summary: A giant panda spends much of its day finding and chewing bamboo. Its heavy jaws break tough stems, and a special wrist bone sticks out where a thumb might be.

cards.title: Why do hockey players use a puck?
cards.summary: Ice hockey players use curved sticks to move a flat rubber puck across the ice. Its flat face lets it slide, which helps players send it along the surface toward a teammate.

cards.title: Why do Japanese readers learn three kinds of signs?
cards.summary: A sentence in Japanese can use three sets of signs. Kanji are characters that often help show the meaning of a word.

cards.title: Why do jigsaws have edge pieces?
cards.summary: In a rectangular jigsaw, the pieces at the outside have at least one straight edge. That makes them easier to sort before you look for a place for each one.

cards.title: Why do Korean letters fit together in blocks?
cards.summary: Hangul is a way to write Korean. It has letters for sounds, but people arrange the letters in square-like groups.

cards.title: Why do leaves change color in fall?
cards.summary: A summer maple leaf looks green because it has a lot of a substance called chlorophyll. In fall, as days get shorter, the leaf makes less chlorophyll and the green color fades.

cards.title: Why do linguists write sounds with the IPA?
cards.summary: A word’s ordinary spelling does not always tell you how it sounds. In English, the letters “sh” work together in “ship” to spell one sound.

cards.title: Why do little maple “helicopters” spin?
cards.summary: Many maples have dry fruits with a thin wing around or beside a pocket holding a seed. When a fruit falls, the wing can make it turn in the air.

cards.title: Why do mancala games use rows of pits?
cards.summary: Mancala is a family of board games that use small pieces and rows of hollow places. In many versions you pick up all the pieces from a pit, then put them down one at a time in later pits as you go around the board.

cards.title: Why do mangrove trees have roots above water?
cards.summary: Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow along warm coasts, often where the tide soaks their roots with seawater. Their roots can grow into shapes that support each tree in muddy ground and help some roots get air.

cards.title: Why do monarch butterflies fly south in autumn?
cards.summary: Many monarchs from eastern parts of North America head south in autumn. They gather in cool mountain forests in central Mexico, where the winter usually lets them survive without laying many eggs.

cards.title: Why do oil-based dressings sometimes separate?
cards.summary: Oil and vinegar can look like a single cloudy liquid after you shake a dressing. The motion breaks the oil into drops and spreads them through the watery vinegar.

cards.title: Why do orchards grow more than one kind of apple tree?
cards.summary: Many apple trees grow more fruit when their flowers receive pollen from a different, compatible kind of apple tree. An orchard can have several kinds flowering around the same time to provide that pollen.

cards.title: Why do peanuts grow underground?
cards.summary: A peanut plant makes flowers above ground, but after flowering it grows a slender part that reaches downward. This part is called a peg.

cards.title: Why do people call many routes the Silk Roads?
cards.summary: The Silk Roads were linked routes between parts of Asia and places farther west. Travelers could choose different roads depending on the season, water, or who controlled a pass.

cards.title: Why do people organize information in a spreadsheet?
cards.summary: A spreadsheet is a table of little spaces arranged in rows and columns. One column could name each fruit your class counts, and another could hold how many you saw.

cards.title: Why do people save seeds in seed banks?
cards.summary: A seed bank stores seeds so people can grow their plants again in the future. It may hold many varieties of one crop.

cards.title: Why do people use money?
cards.summary: Money makes it easier to buy and sell things. Imagine you make a hat and want a book.

cards.title: Why do people use the same language in different ways?
cards.summary: A dialect is a form of a language used by a group of people. Their words, pronunciation, or ways of putting words together can differ from another group’s.

cards.title: Why do plants have stems?
cards.summary: A stem holds plant parts in places where they can do their jobs. A tall stem can lift leaves toward the light.

cards.title: Why do plants release water vapor?
cards.summary: Water from damp cells inside a leaf can turn into vapor. That vapor escapes through small openings called stomata.

cards.title: Why do programs use functions?
cards.summary: A program can give a name to a group of steps it may use again. One name for that group is a function.

cards.title: Why do programs use loops?
cards.summary: A loop tells a program to go through the same group of steps more than once. An animation might use a loop to move a picture a little, show it, and move it again.

cards.title: Why do rolled oats look flat?
cards.summary: An oat grain starts inside a tough covering that people remove before cooking it. The edible part left behind is a groat.

cards.title: Why do shoots sometimes bend toward a window?
cards.summary: A young stem beside a window can bend as it grows. The side away from the strongest light can stretch more than the lit side.

cards.title: Why do snowflakes usually have six sides?
cards.summary: A snowflake begins when water forms a tiny ice crystal in a cold cloud. Water molecules fit together in a repeating pattern in ice.

cards.title: Why do some Buddhist towers have stacked roofs?
cards.summary: A pagoda is a tower found in parts of Asia. In many examples, each level has a wide roof or ledge that makes the tower look like a stack.

cards.title: Why do some ferns have dots under their leaves?
cards.summary: Turn over a mature leaf on some ferns and you may see rows of round brown spots. The spots are groups of tiny cases that hold spores.

cards.title: Why do some filenames end in .jpg or .txt?
cards.summary: The end of a filename after a dot often tells you what kind of file it is. For example, .jpg commonly names one kind of picture file, and .txt often names plain text.

cards.title: Why do some garden plants need a trellis?
cards.summary: A climbing plant may be good at reaching upward but have a stem too thin to stand high on its own. A frame called a trellis gives the stem or its little climbing parts places to grip.

cards.title: Why do some orchid flowers have surprising shapes?
cards.summary: Some orchid flowers have a broad part that gives an insect a place to land. Other parts can point into a space the visitor must pass through.

cards.title: Why do some rice fields look like ponds?
cards.summary: Some farmers place shallow water over a rice field during part of the growing season. Rice can grow in conditions that slow down some weeds, so standing water can help keep a field from getting crowded.

cards.title: Why do some rows curve around the side of a hill?
cards.summary: Water can run quickly down a field if rows lead straight downhill. Planting across the slope makes the rows follow the curves of the hill at about the same height.

cards.title: Why do some soils feel gritty or sticky?
cards.summary: Soil contains mineral pieces of different sizes. Sand has the largest of the three common groups, so it often feels gritty.

cards.title: Why do some water drops leave white spots?
cards.summary: As rain or groundwater moves through rocks, it can pick up small amounts of minerals. Water with a lot of dissolved calcium or magnesium is called hard water.

cards.title: Why do some words rhyme?
cards.summary: The words light and kite rhyme because their stressed vowel and the sounds after it match. The spelling can be different, as it is in blue and through.

cards.title: Why do some words sound alike but mean different things?
cards.summary: Think of “pair” and “pear.” In many English accents, both words sound the same. One refers to two things and the other to a fruit.

cards.title: Why do water drops hold together?
cards.summary: Water molecules tug on other water molecules near them. A molecule deep in water is pulled from many directions.

cards.title: Why do water drops roll off a lotus leaf?
cards.summary: A lotus leaf can look smooth from a distance. Up close, its surface has tiny bumps and a waxy coating.

cards.title: Why do writers give objects feelings?
cards.summary: Personification gives a human action or feeling to something that is not human. The sentence “the sun peeked through the clouds” makes sunlight seem to act like a shy person looking around a corner.

cards.title: Why do xylophones have bars of different sizes?
cards.summary: A xylophone has bars that ring out when a player taps them with mallets. The bars are often wooden, and differences in their lengths and shapes help give them different pitches.

cards.title: Why do you have a pancreas?
cards.summary: The pancreas is a flat organ behind the stomach. It makes liquids containing helpers called enzymes.

cards.title: Why do you need a password?
cards.summary: A password is a secret you enter to help show you are allowed to sign in to an account. If someone else learns it, they may be able to sign in as you.

cards.title: Why do you need a skeleton?
cards.summary: Your skeleton gives your body shape and holds it up when you stand. It gives muscles something firm to pull on when you run, wave, or chew.

cards.title: Why do your eyes make tears?
cards.summary: Your eyes need a thin coat of liquid for more than crying. Each blink spreads a fresh layer of tears across the eye.

cards.title: Why do your pupils change size?
cards.summary: Walk from a sunny yard into a dim room and your eyes start to adjust. The small dark opening in each eye is its pupil.

cards.title: Why do your teeth have different shapes?
cards.summary: When you bite an apple, a flat tooth near the front can cut off a thin piece. The pointier teeth beside the front ones can help hold or tear what you bite.

cards.title: Why does a badminton shuttle slow down so fast?
cards.summary: A badminton shuttle has a rounded base and a wide skirt made from feathers or a shaped material. A racket strikes the base.

cards.title: Why does a cello sound lower than a violin?
cards.summary: A cello has long strings and a large wooden body. Its strings are tuned to make lower notes than the strings of a violin, and the body helps those sounds reach the air.

cards.title: Why does a chess knight move in an L?
cards.summary: The knight in chess looks like a horse’s head. Its move ends two squares away in one direction and one square to the side.

cards.title: Why does a clarinet need a reed?
cards.summary: On a clarinet, a thin strip called a reed sits against a mouthpiece. When a player blows, the reed flexes quickly and sets the air in the tube vibrating.

cards.title: Why does a computer ask to update?
cards.summary: An update is a newer version of part of a program or device. Sometimes it adds something people can use.

cards.title: Why does a digit’s place matter?
cards.summary: In 342, the 3 means three hundreds, the 4 means four tens, and the 2 means two ones. The same digit can be worth a different amount in another place.

cards.title: Why does a flying buttress look like a bridge beside a wall?
cards.summary: A tall stone ceiling can push sideways on its walls as well as down. A flying buttress carries some of that sideways push away from the upper wall across an open space to a strong stone support.

cards.title: Why does a geyser erupt over and over?
cards.summary: A geyser has a narrow or twisted route below ground to water heated by nearby hot rocks. Water deeper down can become very hot under the weight of water above it.

cards.title: Why does a gray whale roll on its side to eat?
cards.summary: A gray whale can feed by turning partly onto its side and drawing in a mouthful of water and mud near the bottom. It pushes the mud and water out through its baleen.

cards.title: Why does a harp have so many strings?
cards.summary: A harp player plucks separate strings to make different notes. Short strings usually make higher sounds than long ones, and strings can also differ in thickness and tightness.

cards.title: Why does a meadow of seagrass matter to fish?
cards.summary: Seagrasses are flowering plants that can live under salty water. Their roots hold onto the sea floor, and long leaves move back and forth when water passes by.

cards.title: Why does a meerkat stand on watch?
cards.summary: Meerkats search for insects and other small animals in open, dry parts of southern Africa. When members of the group dig or look closely at the ground, one may climb onto a high spot and watch for danger.

cards.title: Why does a river sometimes spread into nearby land?
cards.summary: Water reaches a river from streams, slopes, rain, and melting snow. If water comes in faster than it can flow away, the river rises.

cards.title: Why does a salt marsh flood twice a day in some places?
cards.summary: A salt marsh is a low, grassy wetland next to the sea. When the tide comes in, seawater covers part of it, then runs out as the tide falls.

cards.title: Why does a sliced apple turn brown?
cards.summary: A freshly cut apple has new surfaces where the fruit’s cells meet the air. An enzyme in those cells helps oxygen take part in changes that form brown-colored material.

cards.title: Why does a story’s setting matter?
cards.summary: The setting is where and when a story happens. Finding a key in an empty school just after closing feels different from finding one in a sunny park at noon.

cards.title: Why does a track cycling course tilt at the sides?
cards.summary: A velodrome is a closed oval track used for bicycle racing. The track is higher near the outside edges of the bends.

cards.title: Why does a trombone have a slide?
cards.summary: A trombone player starts a sound by buzzing their lips into the mouthpiece. The slide is made of tubes that can move into or out of other tubes.

cards.title: Why does a wool sweater help keep you warm?
cards.summary: Wool comes from the coat of an animal, often a sheep. Its fine fibers often have little bends or waves.

cards.title: Why does an app ask to use your camera or location?
cards.summary: An app sometimes asks to use a tool or information on your device. A family video call app may need the camera to show your face.

cards.title: Why does an idiom mean more than its words say?
cards.summary: An idiom is an expression people know as a group of words. Its usual meaning can be different from what the words would describe on their own.

cards.title: Why does an oboe use two reeds?
cards.summary: An oboe player blows between two very thin pieces of cane. They are tied together near the base and can move quickly against one another at the tip.

cards.title: Why does an old nail turn rusty?
cards.summary: Iron can slowly react with oxygen when water is present. Some of the iron becomes new compounds containing iron and oxygen.

cards.title: Why does Archaeopteryx look like both a bird and a dinosaur?
cards.summary: An Archaeopteryx fossil can show feather marks beside the bones. The long feathers on the wings look much like some bird feathers today.

cards.title: Why does clear egg white turn solid as it cooks?
cards.summary: An uncooked egg white is a watery mixture with many folded proteins in it. Heat makes some of those proteins unfold and catch on to one another.

cards.title: Why does extra sugar stay on the bottom?
cards.summary: At a given temperature, a glass of water can hold only a certain amount of dissolved sugar. When it holds as much as it can, the solution is saturated.

cards.title: Why does garlic come apart into cloves?
cards.summary: The round piece of garlic in a kitchen is a bulb. Peel away its dry outer covering and you can see several smaller pieces called cloves.

cards.title: Why does Hokusai’s Great Wave look so large?
cards.summary: In Hokusai’s print of a great wave off Kanagawa, the dark blue wave curls over boats close to the front of the picture. Japan’s Mount Fuji looks tiny in the background, although a mountain is much bigger than a wave.

cards.title: Why does ice float on liquid water?
cards.summary: In liquid water, molecules can move and slip close to one another. When ordinary ice forms, the molecules lock into a regular arrangement with more open space.

cards.title: Why does plywood have layers that face different ways?
cards.summary: A piece of solid wood often splits more easily in the direction its fibers run. In plywood, a panel is made by gluing together thin sheets of wood.

cards.title: Why does soda fizz when you open it?
cards.summary: A bottle of soda holds carbon dioxide mixed into the liquid. Inside the closed bottle, the gas above the drink pushes on the liquid.

cards.title: Why does some volcanic rock look like glass?
cards.summary: Obsidian is a natural glass that can form when some kinds of lava cool quickly. The material becomes solid before crystals have time to grow very much.

cards.title: Why does sweating cool you down?
cards.summary: Your body can make sweat when you get warm. The sweat spreads across your skin.

cards.title: Why does thawed fruit sometimes feel softer?
cards.summary: Inside a piece of fruit, little cells hold water and other materials. When fruit freezes, some of that water becomes ice crystals.

cards.title: Why does the Mona Lisa’s face look so softly shaded?
cards.summary: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa as a portrait. Around the eyes and mouth, the changes from light to dark are very gentle.

cards.title: Why does the United States take a census?
cards.summary: A census counts the people who live in a place. The United States takes a census of the whole country once every ten years.

cards.title: Why does toast turn brown when it heats?
cards.summary: When a bread surface gets hot, some of its sugars react with pieces of proteins. These changes make new substances that can give toast its brown color and warm smell.

cards.title: Why does water bubble when it boils?
cards.summary: As water heats, more of its molecules can move into a gas. At the boiling point, bubbles of water vapor can grow inside the liquid and reach the surface.

cards.title: Why does Wonderland play with words and rules?
cards.summary: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, an English writer who also taught mathematics. In Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, Alice meets characters who give strange answers to ordinary questions.

cards.title: Why does your body need iron?
cards.summary: Iron is a metal that can be part of materials in your body, even though it does not look like a nail or a piece of steel there. Red blood cells use it in hemoglobin, which picks up oxygen as blood flows past the lungs.

cards.title: Why does your body need protein?
cards.summary: Protein does many jobs in the body. Some proteins help form muscles.

cards.title: Why does your body need vitamins?
cards.summary: Vitamins are substances you need in small amounts. Different vitamins help with different jobs.

cards.title: Why does your body need water?
cards.summary: Water is part of your blood and of the cells all through your body. It helps carry materials and helps you stay at a workable temperature.

cards.title: Why doesn’t some art look like real things?
cards.summary: Some artists start with a real object and change its shapes, colors, or details. A bicycle might become a few circles and slanting lines.

cards.title: Why don’t oil and water mix evenly?
cards.summary: In water, the parts of each molecule that pull on nearby molecules help water gather together. Oil molecules do not make the same strong connections with water.

cards.title: Why Earth has seasons
cards.summary: Earth has seasons because the line it spins around is tilted. During part of the year, the northern half leans toward the Sun.

cards.title: Why electric toaster wires glow
cards.summary: Inside a toaster, electric current travels through narrow heating elements. The elements resist the motion of charge, so some of the electrical energy becomes warmth in the metal.

cards.title: Why electricity changes voltage along the way
cards.summary: A transformer normally has two coils of wire arranged around a shared piece of magnetic material. Current changing direction in the first coil makes its magnetic field change too.

cards.title: Why friction helps us walk
cards.summary: When you step forward, your shoe presses backward on the ground for a moment. Friction is the force between the shoe and ground that helps keep the shoe from sliding.

cards.title: Why high-speed trains need special tracks
cards.summary: Fast passenger trains such as Japan’s Shinkansen use carefully built routes. Gentle curves help keep the sideways pull small at speed.

cards.title: Why is a double bass so big?
cards.summary: The double bass is the largest of the string instruments usually found in an orchestra. Its long, thick strings can move back and forth slowly enough to give it very low notes.

cards.title: Why is a glacial valley shaped like a U?
cards.summary: A river often cuts a narrow trench with sloping sides. A glacier can fill much more of that valley and rub against its bottom and sides.

cards.title: Why is a nautilus shell divided into rooms?
cards.summary: A chambered nautilus is an ocean animal with a coiled shell divided by walls. Its soft body lives in the large room near the opening.

cards.title: Why is a tomato a fruit?
cards.summary: In a tomato flower, a small part where seeds can develop, called the ovary grows into the tomato. That makes a tomato a fruit in botany, the study of plants.

cards.title: Why is an elephant seal named for an elephant?
cards.summary: An adult male northern elephant seal has a large nose that hangs over its mouth a little like a short trunk. It helps make the seal’s deep calls loud during the breeding season.

cards.title: Why is an ice cream cone shaped like a cone?
cards.summary: A round cone has a circular base and a surface that gets narrower until it reaches a point. An empty ice cream cone is like the hollow side of that solid shape.

cards.title: Why is bamboo a grass when it looks like a tree?
cards.summary: Bamboo can grow tall, hard stems that look almost like small tree trunks. It is still in the grass family, along with lawn grass, wheat and rice.

cards.title: Why is calcium important for bones?
cards.summary: Calcium is a mineral nutrient. Inside your body, much of it goes into the hard material in bones and teeth.

cards.title: Why is Cherokee removal remembered as the Trail of Tears?
cards.summary: In the late 1830s, the United States government forced most Cherokee people in the southeastern United States to leave their homes. Soldiers gathered families, and groups traveled to lands far to the west.

cards.title: Why is Deinonychus called a terrible claw?
cards.summary: Deinonychus had a large, sharply curved claw on one toe of each foot. Its name means terrible claw.

cards.title: Why is DNA compared to a twisted ladder?
cards.summary: Think of a ladder with two long sides and rungs in between. A DNA molecule has two sides made of repeating parts.

cards.title: Why is grass wet on a morning when it did not rain?
cards.summary: After sunset, a blade of grass can cool more quickly than the air a little above it. Air touching the blade also cools.

cards.title: Why is it called a green sea turtle?
cards.summary: A green sea turtle’s name comes from the green tint of its body fat, rather than the outside of its shell. Older green turtles often graze on seagrasses and algae in shallow water.

cards.title: Why is it hard to see colors in the dark?
cards.summary: Look at colorful things in a bright room and then in the same room after it gets dim. You may still make out shapes after a while, but colors are harder to notice.

cards.title: Why is Louis Armstrong remembered in jazz?
cards.summary: Louis Armstrong grew up in New Orleans and became a celebrated jazz trumpeter and singer. He could take a tune listeners recognized and change the way some notes fell on the beat.

cards.title: Why is most of an iceberg under water?
cards.summary: Icebergs form when pieces break off a glacier or a floating extension of one. An iceberg’s ice is usually made from snow that fell on land, so it is mostly fresh water.

cards.title: Why is the golden frog bright yellow?
cards.summary: The Panamanian golden frog is a small toad with bright yellow skin that often has dark marks. The bright color can warn other animals that the skin contains chemicals they should avoid.

cards.title: Why is yogurt thicker than milk?
cards.summary: In yogurt making, certain helpful bacteria use some of the sugar in milk and produce lactic acid. The acid makes the milk more sour.

cards.title: Why keep a backup copy of a file?
cards.summary: A backup is an extra copy that helps you get a file back if something happens to the one you use. If a drawing is saved in one place and both your computer and the drawing disappear, you have no second copy there.

cards.title: Why light cannot escape a black hole
cards.summary: A black hole is a place where so much mass is packed into a small region that, past a certain boundary, nothing can get back out. This boundary is the event horizon.

cards.title: Why many meteors can appear on one night
cards.summary: A meteor is the bright streak we see when a small piece of material enters Earth’s air very fast. At certain times of year, Earth crosses trails of dust left by comets.

cards.title: Why might a web page load faster the second time?
cards.summary: The first time a browser shows a page, it may ask for the text, pictures, and other parts separately. It can keep copies of some of those parts in a space called a cache.

cards.title: Why mirrors show a clear image
cards.summary: Ordinary walls bounce light in many directions. A smooth mirror sends much of that light in a more orderly way.

cards.title: Why mix one metal with other elements?
cards.summary: An alloy contains at least one metal mixed with other elements. The mixture can behave differently from the pure metal.

cards.title: Why pendulums swing back and forth
cards.summary: A pendulum is a weight hanging from a string or rod that can move side to side. If the weight is lifted and released, gravity pulls it toward the lowest point.

cards.title: Why plant a crop that you may not harvest?
cards.summary: A cover crop is grown to do a job for the soil. Its leaves and roots can protect a field when a main crop is out of season.

cards.title: Why Pluto is a dwarf planet
cards.summary: Pluto is a small world of rock and ice that goes around the Sun. It is round like a planet, but its gravity does not control its path’s neighborhood.

cards.title: Why repeat the first sound of words?
cards.summary: When nearby words begin with the same sound, the effect is called alliteration. Say “soft snow slipped past” and listen to the repeated s sound.

cards.title: Why some days are longer than others
cards.summary: Earth’s axis is tilted as our planet travels around the Sun. Around the June solstice, the north half leans most toward the Sun and has its longest days.

cards.title: Why some electrical problems turn the power off
cards.summary: A wire can heat up if more electric current passes through it than it was made to carry. A protective device called a circuit breaker can open the wire’s path automatically.

cards.title: Why some gardens are planted lower than the ground
cards.summary: A rain garden looks like a shallow hollow planted with things that can handle occasional wet soil. Water rushing off a roof, road or path can spread out and slow down in the hollow.

cards.title: Why staying over your feet helps you balance
cards.summary: Imagine a straight line drawn downward from the place where your weight is balanced. When that line falls between your feet, your body can often stay steady.

cards.title: Why steel ships can float
cards.summary: A steel nail sinks, but a ship made of steel can float because the hull takes up much more space than the steel alone. The wide hull keeps water out of air-filled spaces.

cards.title: Why sunsets can turn red or orange
cards.summary: At sunset, the Sun is low on the horizon. Its light travels a longer, slanted path through the lower atmosphere than it did at midday.

cards.title: Why the ground shakes in an earthquake
cards.summary: An earthquake can start when rocks on each side of a break in Earth’s crust get stuck. The break is called a fault.

cards.title: Why the Moon can turn red during an eclipse
cards.summary: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the Sun and the full Moon so that the Moon moves through Earth’s shadow. In a total eclipse, most direct sunlight is blocked from reaching it.

cards.title: Why the Moon changes shape in the sky
cards.summary: The Moon is always round, even when it looks like a thin slice. Usually, sunlight lights up one half of the Moon.

cards.title: Why the Moon keeps the same face toward Earth
cards.summary: The Moon spins once during each trip around Earth. Because the two motions take the same time, nearly the same side stays pointed toward us.

cards.title: Why the ocean has tides
cards.summary: If you leave a stick on the beach, later waves might reach it even though the wind has not changed. The water level rises and falls as part of the tide.

cards.title: Why there are waves in the ocean
cards.summary: Many ocean waves begin when wind pushes on the water’s surface. The pushes add energy.

cards.title: Why tiny rolling balls help wheels turn
cards.summary: In a machine, a wheel sometimes has to turn while a nearby part stays still. If their surfaces slide directly against each other, they can waste energy as heat and gradually wear down.

cards.title: Why volcanoes erupt
cards.summary: A volcano has an opening where hot melted rock can reach Earth’s surface. The melted rock is called magma while it is below ground and lava once it comes out.

cards.title: Why was Berlin once divided by a wall?
cards.summary: After the Second World War, Germany and the city of Berlin were split into areas controlled by different governments. In 1961, East German leaders built a barrier through and around West Berlin to stop people from leaving across the city’s border.

cards.title: Why was Rosa Parks’s bus ride important?
cards.summary: Rosa Parks had worked for civil rights for years before she was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1955. On a city bus, a driver told her to give up her seat under rules that separated riders by race.

cards.title: Why was the Great Pyramid built?
cards.summary: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built as a tomb for Khufu, a ruler of ancient Egypt. It rises from a broad, square base and has four sides that slope toward the top.

cards.title: Why was the Taj Mahal built?
cards.summary: The Mughal ruler Shah Jahan had the Taj Mahal built in Agra, India, to honor his wife Mumtaz Mahal after she died. It includes a tomb, gardens, waterways, and several other structures.

cards.title: Why was Yellowstone made a national park?
cards.summary: Yellowstone became a national park in 1872. An important reason was that people wanted to keep its geysers, hot springs, and other unusual natural features protected and open to visitors.

cards.title: Why water towers are so tall
cards.summary: A water tower holds a tank high above the ground. Pumps fill the tank when they can, and gravity helps push its stored water down into the town’s pipes.

cards.title: Why were Hammurabi’s laws carved in stone?
cards.summary: Hammurabi was a king of Babylon who had rulings carved into a tall dark stone almost four thousand years ago. The small wedge marks give examples of disputes and punishments.

cards.title: Why were the Federalist Papers written?
cards.summary: After delegates proposed the Constitution in 1787, the states had to decide whether to approve it. Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay wrote essays to persuade people to support the plan.

cards.title: Why would an online picture have a text description?
cards.summary: A page can give a picture a short description called alt text. A screen reader can speak those words so someone can understand the part the picture plays even when they cannot see it.

cards.title: Why would people build a bridge for animals?
cards.summary: A road can cut between places where animals eat, drink, or raise young. A bridge covered with soil and plants can let some animals cross above moving cars.

cards.title: Will saved seeds grow into the same kind of plant?
cards.summary: A saved seed can start another plant, but the new plant may not be exactly like the old one. In many kinds of plants, pollen can come from a second plant, and the new seed can carry a mix of traits.

cards.title: Zambia
cards.summary: Zambia is a landlocked country in southern Africa, mostly on a raised plateau. Lusaka, the capital, lies in the south-central part of the country.

cards.title: Zimbabwe
cards.summary: Zimbabwe is an inland country on a high area of southern Africa between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers. Harare, the capital, sits on higher ground inland.
